title: Council Post: Overcoming The Challenges Of Using AI Chatbots In Healthcare
text:
Klaudia Zaika is the CEO of Apriorit, a software development company that provides engineering services globally to tech companies.
Healthcare organizations are struggling with high demand for medical services and short staffing. This makes healthcare professionals overworked, burned out and tempted to leave their jobs. Many believe that AI-based solutions like chatbots can reduce the load on healthcare professionals and make medical help more accessible to patients.
However, patients and doctors are reluctant to adopt AI technology. Sixty percent of U.S. patients are uncomfortable with receiving AI-based diagnosis and treatment, while doctors point out that using popular AI tools like ChatGPT can worsen the quality of healthcare services.
My company also faces challenges related to the accuracy and security of AI chatbots in our attempts to make them reliable tools for healthcare organizations. Today, I want to share our experience and assure you that those challenges should not restrain you from leveraging generative AI for the benefit of your business.
Benefits And Risks Of Using Out-Of-The-Box AI Chatbots
Today, AI chatbots are widely used for simple administrative tasks like scheduling appointments and providing basic information about services. However, their capabilities in healthcare can go far beyond that. An AI chatbot can diagnose patients, prepare and consult on treatment plans and provide other personalized care and informational support 24/7. Chatbots can even do these tasks at a professional level: Google’s Med-PaLM reached the level of a human expert in answering U.S. Medical Licensing Examination-style questions.
There are a lot of benefits to using AI chatbots for more sophisticated use cases.
• Improving the reach of healthcare services.
• Providing medical help to patients who can’t usually access it.
• Reducing the load on healthcare professionals.
• Reaching a wider net of patients.
Despite these benefits, many healthcare organizations are still reluctant to implement AI chatbots because of the risks of using a solution without sufficient training and customization. These risks often include:
• Incorrect diagnosis and mistreatment.
• Biased treatment.
• Increased workload for security professionals.
• Lawsuits, fines and loss of reputation.
• Data security issues.
The good thing is that you can train an AI chatbot to reduce the possibility of these risks. My company often works with clients who want to use customized AI tools, including chatbots. There are several development practices that help us make sure we deliver solutions that drive their businesses forward.
Customize An AI Chatbot With Your Training Database
Any AI solution has to be trained on a set of data before it can be released. Training helps an AI algorithm learn new information and prepare for the tasks it’s supposed to perform. Extensive training with a custom set of medical data helps a chatbot provide accurate answers.
Luckily, medical organizations harbor tons of valuable data like patient requests, treatment histories, medical research and test results. Doctors can cooperate with developers to create a database adjusted to the needs of a particular organization. Developers with experience in working with AI can help you:
• Establish and support consistent data labeling and annotation formats.
• Minimize the risk of bias in data that can lead to discrimination in an AI chatbot’s work.
• Anonymize patient data to ensure privacy.
Teach Your AI Chatbot To Say, “I Don’t Know”
One key issue of generative AI tools like chatbots is hallucination—cases where the AI confidently provides a false answer. They happen because an algorithm doesn’t have data to answer a user prompt correctly and starts behaving like a student caught without their homework.
In healthcare, hallucinations by AI chatbots can result in wrong diagnoses, mistreatment, and misinformation of patients. All of these can lead to lawsuits, fines and penalties—or even to the closure of a healthcare institution.
The good news is that you can customize chatbot behavior by adding instructions to prompts. These instructions can clarify the AI’s role and intention in the conversation, urge the AI to ask more questions or acknowledge if it doesn’t know the answer and motivate the user to contact a doctor.
Customizing chatbot behavior also helps to clearly define the roles and responsibilities between an AI chatbot and a healthcare professional. However intelligent it may be, a chatbot can’t substitute a trained doctor. You can instruct a chatbot to urge a user to see a doctor when it obtains information about particular symptoms, chronic conditions or medical history details.
Strengthen AI Chatbot Security
AI chatbots may have access to a lot of sensitive data both during training and in use. They collect patients’ symptoms and histories, manage test results, facilitate communication between doctors and patients and more. Implementing features that help secure medical data and access to it helps you to increase patients’ trust in your chatbot and comply with HIPAA, PIPEDA, GDPR and other data protection laws and regulations.
There are several ways to improve the security of an AI chatbot.
• Limit the chatbot’s access to sensitive records so that it can interact only with data it needs.
• Minimize the amount of personal health information the chatbot stores.
• Implement encryption algorithms for data that your AI chatbot collects from patients.
• Define the list of employees and user roles the chatbot can share sensitive information with.
Also, it’s a good idea to regularly test an AI chatbot’s protection measures and response to malicious requests. Generative AI is a rapidly developing technology, and hackers constantly come up with new ways to abuse it. Regular audits help to ensure that your healthcare data stays protected over time.
When my company works on any AI chatbot for a client who operates with sensitive data, we always include these practices in our development process. Experienced AI developers have already figured out how to mitigate the challenges of using AI in high-risk industries. Thanks to that, healthcare organizations can focus on improving their services with AI and improving patient care.

title: Council Post: Reimagine Customer Experience, Risk And Regulation In Financial Services With AI
text:
Zehra Cataltepe is the CEO of TAZI.AI, an adaptive, explainable AI and Generative AI platform. She has more than 100 AI papers and patents.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) are reshaping the financial services landscape. Beyond enhancing customer experience, AI is transforming regulatory compliance, risk management and core business strategies. I aim to explore the tangible ways AI is revolutionizing the heavily regulated financial industry, focusing on how AI can be leveraged to improve both customer outcomes and regulatory adherence.
1. AI: A New Frontier For Customer Experience And Risk Management
AI is dramatically improving customer experience in financial services. Through personalized recommendations, real-time support and efficient issue resolution, AI is enabling institutions to understand customer needs and prioritize digital transformation initiatives that resonate with them. AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants are becoming table stakes in addressing customer inquiries promptly.
AI's predictive capabilities extend beyond customer service. By analyzing customer communications and complaints, AI models can anticipate which interactions might escalate, flag potential AML or other fraud issues and identify emerging trends in customer behavior, feedback or regulatory problems. This proactive approach allows institutions to mitigate risk, protect customers and improve customer experience.
2. Simplifying AI Adoption: From Executives To Agile Development
As an executive, you don't need to be an AI expert to harness its power, so no need for that Python-based AI class. Today, a range of out-of-the-box AI solutions exist to address specific business requirements, such as retention, demand or fraud.
Your most important role as an executive is helping your team prioritize their efforts with the right AI solution KPIs and making sure that your teams follow an agile solution development cycle, which will allow you to see results in weeks, not months or years. Quicker results and tangible returns on investment get you the must-have board-level support and continued investment.
Here are two reasons why you can get results so fast now:
• Some GenAI solutions ensure data privacy by processing information locally, mitigating concerns about cloud security.
• GenAI is adding to agility by transforming the way AI solutions are created. For example, at my company, we can create initial solutions both for structured and unstructured data easily, thanks to LLMs' capability to process both. GenAI is reducing the time spent for the initial value by reducing or zeroing the training data requirements.
You can start with a prompt that describes the problem to be solved and helpful insights, such as notable segments of different customers retained and churned. Considering the months spent processing the transactional data required to train the initial AI models, this is a huge breakthrough.
3. Breaking Down Silos And Reimagining Customer Complaints
Traditionally, customer complaints were viewed as a regulatory burden. However, AI-powered tools can analyze complaints holistically, identifying root causes and trends. By integrating complaint data with other customer communications and internal transactional data, institutions can prioritize issues that greatly impact customer experience and regulatory compliance, and make business decisions based on customer churn, risk and lifetime value prediction models.
AI and GenAI models deployed throughout the organization are dismantling data silos that have long hindered progress. By integrating information from various sources, institutions can generate valuable insights with AI, even with incomplete data. This is transformative in areas like mortgage and wealth management, where data integration has been a costly challenge.
4. Board-Level Considerations And Organizational Alignment
Implementing AI successfully requires alignment across the organization. KPIs, incentives and compensation plans will need to be adjusted to encourage collaboration and data sharing. Additionally, organizational structures may need to be reevaluated to ensure that AI projects are prioritized and integrated effectively.
Actually, all board-level discussions should focus on incentivizing collaboration between departments. For instance, improving customer lifetime value can become a shared KPI across departments such as fraud, marketing, sales and customer support, encouraging a unified approach to customer-centric strategies.
Conclusion
AI and GenAI are revolutionizing the financial services customer experience, risk management and regulatory compliance. Today, gaining value from AI and GenAI doesn't require massive amounts of time, data, computational resources or deep expertise.
Financial institutions that embrace AI in an agile, holistic and compliant manner will be able to move quickly. This approach will not only enhance customer satisfaction but also provide an unparalleled competitive edge in an increasingly digital world.

title: Go Small To Go Big: Small Wins Prove AI Isn’t A Bubble
text:
The overarching narrative of AI being a bubble is rooted in the idea that behind all the NVIDIA GPUs shipping to hyperscalers there is a nearly non-existent demand for AI.
At first glance, the idea that Meta Platforms Inc., Alphabet Inc.’s Google, Amazon.com Inc., Tesla Inc., and other companies would spend more than $100 billion in capex on AI infrastructure (sell-In) without a clear view of what customers are going to do with it (sell-out) is almost absurd. However, there are very smart people in Venture Capital and financial services at firms like Sequoia and Goldman Sachs that are suggesting AI, at least at this current juncture, is a bubble.
Is there an AI Bubble?
The answer depends on the timetable by which you measure AI and its impact on industries.
First, historically speaking, AI algorithms are more than four decades old, and the tech industry has been investing heavily in variants of artificial intelligence such as machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, and more extensively for at least 10 to 15 years.
Generative AI, and its late 2022 arrival, changed the timeline and gave a glimpse of what felt like a more prescient type of AI that generated text, images, then video, and now a variety of outputs — providing a sneak peek at what we refer to as Artificial General Intelligence, the holy grail or end of days depending on whom you talk to.
Today, the market is seeking to better understand how the sell-in of GPUs and XPUs at a pace of more than $100 billion in 2024, and growing, is going to convert to value outside of the tech industry.
For instance, AI is showing up at banks, hospitals, hotels, manufacturing plants, transportation, retail, and more. The bear thesis is AI is mostly hype, with limited evolution from the data optimization tactics of the past 15 years and that customers aren't going to pay more for SaaS services with Generative AI capabilities or new PCs and smartphones with AI features.
Our intelligence data suggests otherwise. What many aren’t accounting for in the AI calculus is the timeline that AI will be digested and deployed, and how that will vary across industries and lead to a variance in time-to-value for many business use cases.
Our data is also showing triple-digit percent increases in multimillion-dollar proof of concepts (POCs) in 2024 and mid- to high- double-digit percentage growth of AI use in key industries like financial services, healthcare, and telco growing near 40% CAGR over the next five years. Use cases like object detection and conversational AI are also seeing more than 35% growth (five-year CAGR), which means the silicon investment and infrastructure build out will have to convert to software and industry use cases. However, it is more of a drip right now. And once the dam breaks, it will become a waterfall.
I've regularly referenced the three AI network effects, and I’ll refer back to them here once again. We are seeing most of the AI impact on the economy in the n0 and n1 effects with increasing small wins for the n2 node. All of this provides a big opportunity for the System Integrator community that is building these POCs and supporting the buildout of AI within the enterprise chip design and manufacturing network (NVIDIA, AMD Inc., Synopsys Inc., TSMC, Arm Holdings, Intel Corp., etc.)
Network One Infrastructure buildout (Dell, Lenovo, Super Micro Computer Inc., AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Corp., etc.)
Network Two Enterprise Software and SaaS + Devices at the edge (Salesforce Inc., Microsoft Corp. apps, Palantir Technologies Inc., SAP, Oracle, ServiceNow Inc., IBM Corp., HP Inc., Dell Inc., Samsung Electronics, Apple Inc., etc.)
Network Three Industry Adoption and Implementation (financial services, manufacturing, healthcare, etc.)
In conclusion, AI and mega cap tech have a different horizon for AI than most investors and certainly traders.
Businesses have been extracting value in AI for years, and generative AI has accelerated demand, increased data volumes, and increased pressure on enterprises to implement AI faster to stay competitive. But the expense of build out and the complexity of the data estate are substantial challenges for most companies, and the tech industry does have an important point to make that AI features are incremental. Customers and consumers are willing to pay for AI features, especially those that have free (often open source) alternatives.
There isn’t really a bubble around AI, but there also aren’t enough big wins for analysts and investors to fully see the economic impact beyond the data center.
I see that changing in the next 18 months. Some may think that is too long, so we’ll have to settle for small wins that keep on coming or perhaps another way of looking at it is when it comes to AI implementations it will be slow at first, and then (nearly) all at once.

title: Callaway Leverages AI With New Apex Ai200, Ai300 And Ti Fusion Irons
text:
From streamlining manufacturing to customer service chatbots, writing letters to Olympic athletes and just about everything in between, artificial intelligence (AI) has become the go-to technology across various industries.
By simulating human intelligence through the use of algorithms, data and computational power, AI can efficiently and effectively present solutions at lightning speeds, but there is still a flaw: the output is dependent on the input.
That’s what Callaway learned as it leveraged AI through its Ai Smart Face technology in the recent Paradym Ai Smoke family. But, like AI technology, Callaway is a quick study and the new Apex Ai iron series is proof of that.
“In the past we were using robot swings (to develop clubs), but humans aren’t robots,” said Zack Oakley, Callaway senior product marketing manager. “AI is a tool—it’s only as good as the input, so the better the input, the better your output from the AI is going to be. With this series, it’s getting better input by using swings from real golfers to help us identify tendencies like where they miss and where they need the most help to get the best performance.”
Available at retail starting August 16, the new Callaway Apex Ai irons feature three sets: Apex Ai200, Apex Ai300 and Apex Ti Fusion. The Apex Ai200 and Apex Ai300 will cost $1,400 for a standard 7-piece set, while the Ti Fusion is $2,100 for a standard 7-piece set.
Engineered for players in the 5-12 handicap range, the Apex Ai200 is heralded as Callaway’s “most complete players distance iron,” which features a forged hollow-body design combined with a Forged 455 Face Cup to provide Tour-level speed, feel and consistency.
Designed for golfers with a 12+ handicap, the more forgiving Apex Ai300 is the brand’s “most complete forged game-improvement iron,” featuring a cavity-back design with a slightly larger profile that aids in performance and forgiveness.
Both the Apex Ai200 and Apex Ai300 feature Callaway’s Ai Smart Face technology, which leverages real golfer swing data combined with artificial intelligence to generate speed and consistency with tight dispersion into greens, while promoting optimized flight and forgiveness. Strategically positioned MIM (metal injection molding) weighting ensures optimal center of gravity for the best launch windows.
“It’s really about serving the player and getting back to our roots and giving them exactly what they need,” Oakley said.
First launched in 2014, the “crown jewel” of the Callaway iron portfolio, the Apex series has seen iterations released in 2016, 2019 and 2021, but this year’s update is its best yet.
Not only does the latest Apex iteration feature the Apex Ai200 and Apex Ai300 irons, but the lineup also includes the ultra-premium Apex Ti Fusion, the brand’s “most advanced iron.”
Featuring an industry-first forged titanium face to prompt faster ball speeds for increased power, the Apex Ti Fusion breaks the tradeoff between a traditional one-piece and two-piece iron by creating more deflection than steel, with more urethane interaction and a forged body.
“Apex has been the crown jewel of the Callaway portfolio for 10 years, so we wanted to do something special this year, something that kind of commemorated that moment and spoke to what Apex is,” Oakley said. “It’s a total performance iron. If you think of Mercedes-Benz and they’ve got AMG, this is the AMG—it’s the total performance package with all the bells and whistles.
“I think it’s our most advanced iron we’ve ever created.”

title: People with ADHD are turning to AI apps to help with tasks. Experts say try it cautiously
text:
People with ADHD are turning to AI apps to help with tasks. Experts say try it cautiously
People who have ADHD are starting to turn to AI to help them break down once-insurmountable tasks like emails, business plans and proofreading
Becky Litvintchouk didn’t think she’d be able to manage the mountain of tasks needed to become an entrepreneur. Every other part of her life has been overwhelming because of ADHD, which can impact her ability to concentrate.
So, she turned to AI. The app Claude helps her decide which contracts made the most sense for her hygienic-wipes business, GetDirty, without having to read them word for word. She also created business plans by telling the generative AI bot what her goals were and having it create steps for her to get there.
“It’s been just massively instrumental. I probably would not be where I am today,” she said of using AI for about two years.
Experts say generative AI tools can help people with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder — who experience difficulties with focusing, organizing and controlling impulses — to get through tasks quicker. But they also caution that it shouldn’t replace traditional treatment for ADHD, and also expressed concerns about potential overreliance and invasion of privacy.
Emily Kircher-Morris, a counselor who focuses on neurodivergent patients, said she’s seen the tools be useful to her clients with ADHD. She even uses them herself since she has ADHD.
Her clients, she said, seem to have varying levels of comfort with the idea of using AI. But for those who take to the technology, “it really can help to hook people in, like, ‘Oh, this is kind of a fancy new thing that catches my interest. And so I really want to dig in and explore it.’”
She also said it's good to use caution. John Mitchell, an associate professor at Duke University School of Medicine, added that AI apps should be used more as “one tool in a toolbox” instead of replacing traditional treatments such as developing organizational skills or taking prescription medications.
“If you’re kind of treading water in your job and AI’s a life preserver, well, that’s great you’re staying above water, but, you know, you still don’t know how to swim,” he said.
Litvintchouk, a married mother of four living in New York City, dropped out of high school and left the workforce — all things that research shows are more likely to happen to people with ADHD, putting them at higher risk of economic instability.
Aside from helping with her business, she uses ChatGPT to help with grocery shopping — another thing that can be fraught for people with ADHD because of the organization and planning skills needed — by having it brainstorm easy-to-prepare recipes with a corresponding grocery list.
When she shared her technique with another mom who also has ADHD, she felt more people needed to know about it, so she started creating videos on TikTok about various AI tools she uses to help manage her ADHD struggles.
“That’s when I was like, you know what? I need to, like, educate people,” she said.
Generative AI tools can help people with ADHD break down big tasks into smaller, more manageable steps. Chatbots can offer specific advice and can sound like you're talking with a human. Some AI apps can also help with reminders and productivity.
Software engineer Bram de Buyser, said he created Goblin.tools with his neurodivergent friends in mind. Its most popular feature is the “magic to-do,” where a user can enter a task and the bot will spit out a to-do list. They can even break down items on the list into smaller tasks.
“I’m not trying to build a cure,” he said, “but something that helps them out (for) two minutes out of the day that they would otherwise struggle with.”
Husson University professor Russell Fulmer describes the research around AI and ADHD as “inconclusive." While experts say they see how artificial intelligence could have a positive impact on the lives of people with anxiety and ADHD, Fulmer said, it may not work perfectly for everyone, like people of color with ADHD.
He pointed to chatbot responses that have been racist and biased at times.
Valese Jones, a publicist and founder of Sincerely Nicole Media, was diagnosed with ADHD as a child and uses AI bots to help with reading and responding to emails and proofreading public relations plans. But its responses don’t always capture who she really is.
“I’m southern, so I talk like a southerner. There are cadences in my writing where you can kind of pick up on the fact that I’m southern, and that’s on purpose,” said Jones, who is Black. “It doesn’t pick up on Black women’s tone, and if you do put in like, 'say it like African American,’ it automatically goes to talking like ‘Malibu’s Most Wanted.’”
And de Buyser said while he sees a future where AI chatbots function more like a personal assistant that is “never tired, never sleeps,” it could also have privacy implications.
“If you say, ‘Oh, I want an AI that gives me personal information and checks my calendar’ and all of that, you are giving that big company access to your emails, your calendar, personal correspondence, essentially your deepest, darkest secrets just so it can give you something useful back,” he warned.

title: Some Actors Will Let AI Replicate Their Voices For Advertisements Under New Union Agreement
text:
Topline
Hollywood’s largest actors union on Wednesday announced it has reached a deal that will allow actors to sell the rights to replicate their voices using artificial intelligence to advertisers on a brand-by-brand basis, one year after use of AI in the film industry helped spark an actors strike that lasted nearly four months.
Key Facts
Through the new agreement, actors can agree to allow certain brands to replicate their voices using AI for audio ads with pre-approved scripts.
Performers will connect with advertisers using Narrative, a third-party platform that works directly with the advertisers to create the audio spots, and can approve or deny requests on the spot.
Performers can specify which brands or industries they are willing to work with, consent on a job-by-job basis and see the proposed audio copy for each ad before they accept the deal, which SAG-AFTRA says "ensures fair compensation and transparency."

Crucial Quote
“This streamlined process allows performers to generate income while maintaining full control over their brand and likeness,” SAG-AFTRA said in a statement.
Key Background
The use of artificial intelligence to replace the work of actors and other creatives in Hollywood has been a point of contention for years as AI becomes more prevalent across industries. Last year, both SAG-AFTRA and the Hollywood writers union, the Writers Guild of America, went on strike to protest a number of issues, chief among them the use of AI. Actors wanted to secure protection for their images and performances from AI and writers wanted to limit the use of artificial intelligence in the writing process. Writers ultimately reached a deal that said AI could not be used to write or rewrite scripts, and that protects writers from having their scripts used to train AI without their consent. The actors’ agreement said performers had to provide explicit consent for their likeness to be used in digital replicas and the union must be involved in any use of synthetic performers—meaning anytime AI is used to fully replace a performer who would have otherwise had to fulfill a role in person.
Tangent
Several big-name celebrities have come forward in the last year to deny their involvement in advertisements that appear to use their name, likeness and voice. Actor Tom Hanks last year said he had "nothing to do with” advertisements for a dental plan that were circulating online using an “AI version of me." CBS News anchor Gayle King last year said she was not involved with a weight loss firm named Artipet that she says "manipulated” an existing video of her “to make it seem like I’m promoting it.” Steve Harvey and Taylor Swift were among the celebrities whose likeness was reportedly being used to promote Medicare scams online, and Luke Combs, Miranda Lambert, Garth Brooks and other country stars had their images used to promote weight loss gummies on Facebook and Instagram.
Contra
Some studios have already used extensive artificial intelligence in productions. Artificial intelligence was used to “de-age” actors Harrison Ford in "Indiana Jones and the Dial of Destiny" and Mark Hamill in "The Mandalorian.” AI has also been used to bring actors into a scene posthumously. Carrie Fisher, for instance, died before finishing filming for "Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker," and CGI was used to compile her scenes. The same was done for Paul Walker in '"Furious 7" and Harold Ramis in “Ghostbusters: Afterlife.”

title: How Tapestry Uses AI, Digital Tech And Stores To Serve Its Customers
text:
Noam Paransky was hired as the chief digital officer for Tapestry—parent company of luxury brands Coach, Kate Spade New York and Stuart Weitzman—in April 2019, months before the Covid-19 pandemic upended retail. As the shut-downs and shut-ins began to subside, Paransky’s title was changed to chief omni and innovation officer as a reflection of how consumers now behave: Engaging with brands both online and in person. I talked with him about how Tapestry is working to connect all of the branding, data and commerce dots with both their customers and their sales associates.
This conversation has been edited for length, clarity and continuity. It was excerpted in the Forbes CMO newsletter.
Tell me about how data use has evolved at Tapestry.
Paransky: Tapestry has always been focused on this intersection and tension between magic and logic. We have amazing brands, we sell emotional products, and how we express our brands and products, that’s fundamentally a creative discipline. But there’s always been this rooting in data, in facts, in information, and that’s evolved a lot over the past 10 or 15 years.
In the old days, it was books of data around product category sales, and customer segmentation, and CRM data, and functional attributes of consumer preferences around the product. Historically, you would’ve sent a design team to Tokyo and see what the girls in Harajuku were doing and wearing.
There’s still value in that, but today we have these ethnographic frameworks that we use around the globe with a number of key cities and various regions. We do a lot of user experience research about how people engage digitally. We do studies of how people shop in the stores, and we mine data to see how all of these things connect. AI can help you unearth insights that you couldn't necessarily easily do, or [were] inherent from the intuition of a few key leaders to then communicate, develop understanding, and then extrapolate that into marketing, creative and product design.
Today, that can be distilled in a lot of different ways. When we look at generative AI and computer vision, what’s fundamentally different is that you can take what’s creative, what’s visual and create data, then synthesize that data and match it up with everything else that we’re doing. Then you can also take insights in data and text, and create creative outputs. This is a fundamental inflection point in this intersection of magic and logic.
How did the pandemic change your strategy?
When we came into the pandemic, a lot of the talk was about digital. Death of the stores, everything is digital. But we saw people very quickly yearning for that human contact that we all took for granted. We had Kate Spade sales associates who were our biggest super fans selling via clienteling out of their closets. That would portend what was to happen once the world opened back up.
Yes, we grew digital significantly. We “caught up” or even leapfrogged where the industry was from a digital sales perspective, but that wasn’t the end game. The end game was really understanding: There’s so much value in this contact. We’ve seen that with people coming back to the stores, but we’ve also taken that as instruction: As we listen, as we leverage data and AI, who are the most expert people about our products, our brands, the consumer, and who’s our best personalization engine?
That’s our sales associates. We’re trying to engage with the sales associates in ever more structured and unstructured ways to get their feedback and knowledge, because ultimately we want digital to be more human. The irony is AI and technology will be an unlock to scale that, but it’s still rooted in human understanding and expertise. All these things become ever more jumbled, but the new tools, the new methodologies are allowing the unlocks to happen.
Right now, how do things break down with sales and traffic between digital and in-store?
We do a ton of research on how people shop around the globe. While there are quite significant regional differences between platforms and behaviors between the U.S., China, Japan, and Europe, engagement is happening in a very circular, asymmetrical way. Ultimately, most of the engagement writ large is happening in digital. A lot of that’s in social channels. A lot of that is not our own content. It’s engaging with influencers or community groups about our brands or the category. The action at volume is happening in digital channels.
Generally in high consideration purchase categories like handbags, the majority of sales are happening in the physical world, but those things are inexorably linked. We find in our research that something like 95%+ of consumers are engaging in both physical and digital. It’s not so much, ‘I’m a digital shopper.’ You might transact digitally, but you’re engaging in the physical world quite a bit with the category, with brands.
As we exited the pandemic, we changed my title and my scope to match how the consumer views the world, which is boundary-less and channel-less. They don’t think, ‘I’m engaging with Coach online.’ They just think, ‘I’m engaging with this brand,’ or ‘I’m dreaming of my next handbag or my next pair of shoes.’ They just don’t see the world in a black-and-white way that we might in some financial report.
How does Tapestry meet the consumer where they are and how they want to engage? How do you tailor that for different people, different generations, different parts of the world?
There’s an overlap of a couple things [that] are really fundamental to leveraging tools and technology, or thinking about strategies. No. 1: Understanding who our consumer is, what they want, what they need at the highest level. Preferences in style, function, colors, comfort, etc. Then we do a lot of ethnographic and psychographic research around how do they shop, why do they shop, where do they shop? That runs the gamut from qualitative research to shop-alongs to visits in their home, looking in closets. Getting to the fundamental DNA of who are they really—not just what they say, but what they do—and then fundamentally connecting those things.
We also do a lot of studies on the transitory aspects of what the consumer journey looks like across various regions. Where are they engaging? It goes way up into these social platforms. How do they spend their time in the social platforms? What are they looking for? What are they engaging with? And therefore, how do we set ourselves up for success in that? Then we do a ton of user experience research. As they come from these digital experiences and these other platforms and ultimately either come to our properties or to the store, what are they looking for? How are they looking to transition from those properties that have different kinds of formats, usability patterns, types of content, and then to our brand worlds in the digital realm.
How do we connect the dots to have high utility and understand the different needs? Some people are ready to shop, and that’s great. A lot of people are just looking to engage with the brand, feel things out, get to know more. So as we’re doing these “brand building” campaigns, what do those experiences look like? How do we connect the dots? Then ultimately, how’s that connect if they’re coming into the store to transact, or look, see, touch, engage with an expert sales associate? And then again, how do we bring that back into the digital experience? How are we taking that expertise from the sales associate, and how are we making that more present in the digital experience as well?
It’s got to be around who are we engaging with and why, and how do our brands and our products fit their needs and purpose, and then how do we connect the dots. There’s a ton of qual and quant to get us there. There’s no level of omniscience here.
How much has this process changed since you came to Tapestry?
Over the past five years, it’s evolved quite a bit. It’s rooted in that magic and logic philosophy and understanding and the desire for that positive tension. We brought in new personnel and made investments in technology. The capabilities of what technology can do, they’ve also helped to unlock some of these activities. We really leaned into it three and a half, four years ago when we launched our acceleration program.
How is what you do different, and why is it important for Tapestry’s brands?
Whether it’s luxury retail, buying a car, or anything else that’s higher consideration and emotional, the journey tends to be longer, more circuitous. There are moments when people want to do research and engagement more digitally, in a private environment where they can go to a lot of different places quickly, flipping between social properties and various influencers and our sites, and then ultimately coming down the path. Unlocking that emotion, that understanding, is fundamentally different in these higher consideration categories.
I think that’s where our sales associates really are the killer app. They understand where function and emotional needs intersect, and are really able to explain that to a consumer in a way that there’s almost no substitute. That is what allows us to compete. It’s having that right product, that right messaging and the sales associates and the experiences that back it up, that fundamentally allows us to work to win in the marketplace. In a lower consideration purchase, these things would be probably less important, but we feel really strongly that it makes a huge difference in the understanding of our products, our brands. The satisfaction that the consumer has about their purchase, and the confidence that they have, is they exit and continue to engage with us.
Tell me about your AI-powered Tell Rexy system.
I’m the father of Tell Rexy. It goes back to our awesome sales associates and the expertise that they have. They are engaging with the consumer one-on-one, day in and day out. We have lots of data, but we have to find that and synthesize it. They know what’s happening right in front of them. We’ve always had basic mechanisms for them to give feedback, but those forms ultimately can’t be very rich. You’re checking boxes and pull-down menus, and you’re getting a very rigid set of data, which is then synthesized, typically by one individual, that’s then presented in some kind of structured way to the organization.
There’s so much knowledge that our associates have and we wanted to get that knowledge across a broad array of topics. There’s seven or eight very broad foundational topics that we’ve encouraged them to give feedback [on]. It’s a very simple tool for them to use, as easy as push-to-talk. The speech gets translated into text. It comes into a large language model, and then we are synthesizing that for knowledge and insights.
There’s a push-based and a pull-based process. There’s a weekly synopsis that goes out to 30, 40 leaders across the organization. It’s structured by areas of feedback, product, consumer experience, marketing, you name it. These are the main insights that came through. They’re pretty rich insights unto themselves because, as opposed to a score, it is bulleted lists of three or four top things that we heard from the associates, and the team can take action on that.
There are a number of things like product design that actually get impacted, but a relatable story [from the] holiday [season], we heard from our sales associates that our music in the stores wasn’t festive enough. We wouldn’t have known that, heard that, processed that without this tool. Twenty-four to 36 hours later, the music was changed, festivity was up, the associates were happy, it was energizing for them. Some of the things are fairly innocuous, but can be important. And then some of these things are very foundational in understanding what’s going on with the consumer.
On the pull-based side, I talk with Rexy on a regular basis. I can ask it any kind of question I want. Just like you would ask ChatGPT a question and it’d be trained on the internet, this is trained on the feedback that we get from the associates. Oftentimes it is rooted in something that I saw in the weekly report, and then I start to have a conversation so I can get a much broader landscape of understanding around the topic. I’m able to drill down into the data and get to an answer that gives me the context that I need.
We’ve got tens of thousands of pieces of feedback through this mechanism in nine or 10 months that we’ve had this up. Sometimes you just want to know, are they asking about this week? Sometimes as you have a conversation, you’re drilling in and you want to understand, has this been going on for a long time, a short period of time. It's just a very different way to get and synthesize information.
You’ve done a lot with AI and digital systems and data so far. Where do you see it going in the next 12 months?
I would say that generally any CMO of any brand would say, ‘We would love to have more rich content to put in front of consumers.’ There’s always been a lot of talk of segmentation and personalization, but for that to actually deliver, we need relevant content. There’s never been enough content to fuel that. I think we’re on the precipice of where generative AI is able to, if not from whole cloth, create or augment content in ways that are relevant and compelling. I think we’re at the last mile. Generally, creatives will know it when they see it. And then for those of us who are technologists, we’re trying to find the best, and tweak it and present it to the creatives and iterate.

title: The Movie Experience In The Age Of AI And The Metaverse Has Arrived
text:
As we stand on the precipice of a new era in entertainment, the fusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and the Metaverse is scripting a revolutionary narrative for the movie experience. Imagine a world where the lines between reality and fiction blur, where viewers are not just spectators but active participants in a cinematic universe that extends beyond the screen. That is why this tantalizing future, a confluence of technology and imagination, reshaping our movie experiences.
Act I: The Rise of AI in Cinematic Storytelling
The role of AI in movies has transcended from being a mere tool for special effects to a dynamic force in storytelling. In this future, AI algorithms assist in scriptwriting, analyzing vast databases of film history to suggest plot twists and character arcs that resonate with audiences. These algorithms become collaborative partners, offering writers a kaleidoscope of possibilities, enriching the narrative tapestry. Moreover, consider dynamic scene changes. Personalized storylines in the Metaverse is the future. In the Metaverse, movies are not one-size-fits-all. AI tailors narratives to individual preferences, creating a personalized story for each viewer. This could mean alternative endings, character storylines branching out based on your previous interactions, or even personalized characters that adapt to your emotional responses, monitored through biometric feedback.
Act II: Immersive Worlds (The Metaverse as a Stage)
The Metaverse converges with cinema to create fully immersive worlds. Imagine donning a VR headset and stepping into the movie, walking alongside characters, exploring their world, and even influencing the storyline. Each viewing becomes a unique journey, a personal adventure that goes beyond passive watching to active experiencing. Imagine AI driven avatars that are the co-stars in your story. In these immersive movie experiences, AI avatars interact with you, responding in real-time to your actions and dialogue. These avatars, powered by advanced AI, exhibit complex emotions and behaviors, making your interactions indistinguishably close to real human encounters. You're no longer just watching a character on screen; you're conversing, empathizing, and engaging with them.
Act III: A Symphony of Senses (Beyond Visual and Auditory)
The future movie experience in the Metaverse is a symphony of senses. With haptic feedback technology, you can feel the rush of a car chase or the gentle breeze in a serene landscape. Scent technology integrates to provide a full sensory experience, from the smell of rain in a dramatic scene to the aroma of food in a culinary adventure. Consider the Emotional Compass, an AI system that understands you. As you traverse these cinematic worlds, AI becomes an emotional compass. It understands and adapts to your emotional state, perhaps altering the storyline's intensity to match your mood or offering narrative pathways that resonate with your current feelings. This empathetic AI ensures that each experience is not just engaging but also emotionally attuned.
Act IV: The Democratization of Movie Creation
The future of movies is not just about consumption but creation. The Metaverse, coupled with AI, democratizes moviemaking. With user-friendly AI tools, anyone can create their cinematic worlds in the Metaverse, telling stories that reflect diverse perspectives and experiences. This democratization leads to a rich tapestry of content, a mosaic of narratives from every corner of the globe. Consider collaborative creation by crowdsourcing the narrative. In this future, moviemaking becomes a collaborative endeavor. Viewers contribute to storylines, suggest scenes, or even design virtual environments. Crowdsourcing in the Metaverse harnesses the collective creativity of its inhabitants, leading to dynamic, ever-evolving story worlds.
Act V: The Ethical Framework (The Ultimate AI Question: Balancing Innovation with Responsibility)
As we embrace this new era, the ethical implications are paramount. Ensuring privacy, preventing misuse of biometric data, and fostering positive and inclusive content in the Metaverse become essential mandates. AI and Metaverse platforms operate within an ethical framework that prioritizes user well-being and promotes a healthy, vibrant movie-watching community.
Epilogue: A Vision of Infinite Possibilities
The future of movie experiences in the age of AI and the Metaverse is a narrative of infinite possibilities. It's a future where technology enhances storytelling, where movies are not just watched but lived, and where every viewer has a stake in the narrative universe. In this future, we transcend the boundaries of the screen, stepping into stories that engage, inspire, and transform. We become part of a global community of storytellers and dreamers, each shaping and reshaping this cinematic multiverse.
Moviemakers are embracing this future, not just as spectators but as active participants in a world where the magic of movies and the power of technology converge to create experiences that are profoundly personal, infinitely varied, and endlessly enchanting. The next scene is ours to script, in a movie experience that goes beyond the imagination, into realms of interactive, immersive, and emotionally resonant storytelling.

title: For All Its Hype, AI Isn’t Driving Cloud Growth (Yet)
text:
The three largest cloud service providers (AWS, Google and Microsoft) recently shared their results from the past quarter. Year-over-year cloud revenue growth at AWS and Microsoft was 19%; at Google Cloud, it was a whopping 29%. The three vendors combined for $65 billion in cloud revenues last quarter. Just to put that in perspective, IBM’s entire revenue in fiscal 2023 was just under $62 billion. If you were to stick to the commonly held belief that these three cloud providers represent about two-thirds of CSP market share, cloud computing is about a $350 billion to $400 billion market.
Notably, each company's cloud computing division was positioned as a big highlight. Additionally, there was a lot of discussion about each vendor’s AI efforts. It is logical to think that AI is a big component of this cloud growth. However, because these providers don’t break down their revenues by workloads, it’s difficult to ascertain exactly how big AI is for them.
The Major Drivers For CSP Growth—Not Including AI
While AI is certainly contributing something to the CSPs’ strong results, I do not believe that the contribution is a major driver quite yet. Instead, the recent momentum in cloud computing is the culmination of many other factors that have been building for some time. So, let’s consider these non-AI cloud growth factors.
- Cloud-native application development — While microservices and containers have been around for quite a while, it took a long time for them to gain momentum. This is mainly because there is just so much old code out there stored in well-managed on-premise virtual machines and bare-metal deployments. Additionally, there was a lot of reluctance in IT organizations to relive the change-management challenges and risks associated with the “big bang” upgrades that were the norm in the early 2000s. So, what we saw was more of a piecemeal re-architecture of applications over time. And, like many gradual processes, enterprises eventually hit a tipping point where there was enough code in the cloud that it made sense to accelerate the deployment effort. This was further accelerated by the appearance of a number of useful low-cost cloud and DevOps management tools.
- Nobody “buys” software anymore — Whether enterprises like it or not, the OpEx buying model is now the default. Yes, we definitely still see CapEx purchases in some contexts—for example in some industry- or machine-specific applications—but the tide has turned. It’s easier to account for the cost of a solution when you have internal alignment for how you buy across the board; over the past five to 10 years, more and more customers have needed to upgrade their enterprise applications often, meaning a switch to subscription pricing. This was not an easy process, and many customers are still working through it. But once you get there in terms of the accounting, that’s one more barrier to the cloud that’s been removed.
- Bespoke enterprise apps are no longer the norm — It’s nice to see that application platform providers are more committed to ensuring that customers don’t get left behind with bespoke customizations. For example, SAP is continuing to invest in programs like RISE with SAP to help customers stay current and migrate to the company’s cloud-based offerings. Customers have been vexed by older enterprise applications that were heavily customized and hard to update. These customers are now breaking that cycle and moving their apps to the cloud. This not only helps organizations stay current, it also makes it easier for their remote employees, customers and partners to use these applications wherever they may be.
- IT operations and security is very hard to do — IT organizations are also being impacted by the large number of workers who are leaving. And it’s becoming harder and harder to replace those individuals with new workers. Add to that the constantly shifting dynamics of IT. For an example, just look at cybersecurity: The threat landscape is constantly evolving, the software to manage it yourself is very expensive and, to make matters worse, IT remains under constant budget scrutiny. With fewer skilled people around to do the work, you need to simplify your IT operations—and moving to the cloud can help with that.
These four factors have been nagging IT teams for years now. Slowly but surely, IT is finally putting some of these issues behind them with cloud migrations. But, of course, their leadership always wants to know: “What’s next?”
How AI Is Poised To Sustain CSP Growth
The answer is that AI growth will sustain cloud computing’s growth trajectory for some time to come. Here are three areas where AI is contributing to current and future cloud computing growth.
- Data lakes and training — AI works better when your data is in order. Yes, the big foundation models churn through lots of unstructured data. But for the fine-tuning and tailored customer experiences that enterprises require when they deliver AI apps, the more the enterprise data is in order, the better. In connection with this, we are starting to see real progress in the creation of data lakes that properly incorporate, aggregate and rationalize data such that AI can use it.
- Machine learning and analytics — To say the least, over the past couple of years much has been made of generative AI, especially in the consumer space. However, enterprises want to be able to better model and predict their business decisions. Fortunately, they have troves of business data and equipment that can feed into machine learning models. While ML doesn’t make the same headlines as generative AI, ML is the larger market today, and it is poised to keep growing rapidly for years to come.
- Innovation and experimentation — Over the next few years, we will also see a lot of money invested by enterprises and VCs in making the most of the AI opportunity. It’s going to take a lot of resources and flexibility. Fortunately, cloud computing is there to help spur these future innovations. Building up the infrastructure to make AI a real business driver will likely prove to be too hard and too expensive for many enterprises, whereas using a cloud approach will bring it into range.
Technology has always been the business of the next cool thing, but it has also always been the business of monetizing the last cool thing. AI and cloud computing are no exception.

title: AI Is Transforming Travel: It’s Getting More Personal
text:
Artificial intelligence is already transforming the travel industry, from the initial spark of inspiration to the final homeward journey. Travel and tourism is a colossal economic engine generating trillions annually. AI, in all its multifaceted forms, is the catalyst propelling this transformation. From the moment a traveler begins their search to the instant they reclaim their luggage, AI is redefining expectations.
A new generation of AI-powered chatbots is streamlining the booking process, handling everything from flight searches and hotel reservations to payment and baggage tracking. Moreover, the industry is embracing automation and robotics to optimize baggage handling and reduce delays. As technology advances, hyper-personalization will become the norm, tailoring every aspect of the travel experience to individual preferences and needs.
However, this digital revolution is being overlaid on a legacy infrastructure that is often outdated and fragile. Systems like the venerable Sabre booking platform and the recent, industry-wide disruption caused by the CrowdStrike Windows update highlight the vulnerabilities within the travel ecosystem. Such incidents, impacting airlines, hotels, banks, and support services, underscore the urgent need for a more robust and integrated technological foundation.
AI Is Transforming Every Aspect of the Travel Experience
Despite the challenges posed by legacy systems, the transformative power of AI is undeniable. The travel industry is undergoing a profound metamorphosis, and AI is at the forefront of this evolution. “AI” however has become the ubiquitous buzzword, promising to revolutionize every industry. While the term itself is broad, its applications within the travel sector are increasingly specific and impactful. Here are just a few examples of how AI is making inroads in various sectors of the travel landscape:
Personalized Travel Experiences: AI-driven recommendation engines are refining the art of personalized travel. Platforms such as Google Travel and TripAdvisor employ machine learning to curate itineraries aligned with individual preferences. Many startups are advancing this by introducing natural language processing to create more intuitive user interactions.
Predictive Analytics and Dynamic Pricing: AI-powered predictive analytics is targeting pricing and sales strategies. Hopper's use of machine learning to forecast flight prices is a prime example. This technology also empowers airlines and hotels to dynamically adjust pricing based on demand, optimizing revenue.
Operational Efficiency and Sustainability: Beyond the consumer interface, AI is driving operational improvements and environmental responsibility. Google’s DeepMind team is helping airlines optimize flight paths using machine learning to dramatically reduce contrails which are a significant contributor to the greenhouse gas emissions of flights. Airlines, intercity rail and bus operators also using AI to optimize fuel and energy consumption and emissions, aligning with the burgeoning sustainable tourism market. Additionally, AI-powered image recognition is streamlining baggage handling, tracing which is a big leap in finding lost luggage quickly.
AI Travel Agent Hyper-personalization is the Future Customer Experience
The traditional travel agent's role has been eroded by search engines. AI is poised to further redefine this function. AI agents can swiftly process complex travel requests, scour multiple platforms, and deliver optimized itineraries. However, the human element remains indispensable. My recent experience with a lost stroller in Athens underscored this. While AI accurately tracked the baggage, the chatbot sent me alerts on my phone, it was the human gate agent on our first leg that caused the initial error and it was the human at the receiving end that was crucial in resolving the issue. This highlights the complementary nature of AI and seasoned human expertise.
While stories about how AI will take jobs, the reality is that the roles will change as they did when the internet and smart phones, apps and mobile payments came on the scene. This new era is creating new roles such as AI Travel Specialists, AI Data Analysts, and AI Experience Designers. These professionals will be instrumental in developing, refining, and optimizing AI systems for the travel industry.
The future is going to get more personal, hyper-personal. By leveraging your data on loyalty programs, credit card benefits, and insurance coverage, AI agents will be able to craft highly tailored travel plans, negotiate on your behalf and even decide which card to use to book to maximize points. These intelligent assistants will anticipate your travel needs and predict how to proceed, from optimal flight and accommodation bookings to curated local experiences (maybe they can score the next Taylor Swift concert or Olympic Games tickets!). Their role will extend beyond the initial booking, ensuring seamless journeys and swift resolutions to unexpected challenges. Whatever helps take the stress out of planning travel especially with groups or families and brings in more joy when things go awry is not only part of the experience but well needed relief.
A Complex Interplay of Technological Advancement and Human Touch
While AI will undoubtedly drive automation and efficiency augmented with robotics and hyper-personalization, the industry must also prioritize human-centric service, the warm human touch that are the cornerstones of hospitality, especially in unfamiliar locales and with unexpected circumstances. Seamless integration of AI and human support will be crucial. Additionally, robust data security and privacy protocols are paramount to build trust with consumers. As AI continues to evolve, it's essential to mitigate risks like hallucinations and ensure that AI systems align with ethical guidelines. Companies that address this delicate balance, offering reliable, personalized, and secure travel experiences, will be the ones who shape the industry and benefit from it. If we’re lucky traveling will get a little less complicated and a little more fun again.

title: AI: Overhyped Fantasy Or Truly The Next Industrial Revolution?
text:
The term “fourth industrial revolution” has been used in recent years to describe the transformative impact that many believe AI and automation will have on human society.
The theory goes that previous industrial revolutions have occurred when hugely disruptive technologies were introduced and swiftly adopted, leading to widespread changes in the way we live and work.
They include mechanization in the 18th century, electrification in the 19th century and digitization in the 20th century. Now, the advent of AI and intelligent automation has kickstarted the next industrial revolution. It promises the most dramatic changes yet as electronic brains capable of operating far more quickly than our own supercharge our productivity, creativity and capability across every field of human endeavor.
At least, that’s what we’re told.
Although I believe AI certainly has the potential to be revolutionary, it can’t be denied that there’s a lot of hype around it. And much of that hype is created by multinational businesses that have staked their future on their ability to sell it to us.
So, will it really be on par with the other great industrial revolutions of the past? Or is this talk of the fourth industrial revolution just hot air from marketers talking up the share price of hugely powerful global corporations? Let’s take a look.
The Fourth Revolution?
When future historians look back at this period in time, will they recognize the adoption of AI into business, society and everyday life as being as transformative as mechanization, electrification or digitization?
Well, there will certainly be some similarities.
For one, many jobs will be changed. Just as mechanization and electrification reduced our need for many occupations centered around manual labor, intelligent automation will reduce our reliance on human workers for many routine information-based tasks. Data entry, technical support or call center workers could find that much of their work will be automated, just like those who gathered crops or operated looms did in the past.
Another similarity can be seen in the opportunities to not just automate existing work but create entirely new products and services. Mechanized manufacturing allowed for mass production of many new goods and products, and digitization and the internet led to the emergence of the digital economy. AI promises to bring us self-driving cars, predictive maintenance, personalized medicine, and many other innovations.
Further reinforcing the idea that we are living through a fourth industrial revolution are the widespread ethical and societal implications of this breakthrough technology.
Mechanization was behind the emergence of many of the ideas we have today around workers’ rights. Digitization saw the first questions asked about privacy and security as it became possible for personal information to be collected, stored and transmitted electronically for the first time.
Now, the potential for AI to be misused, including the dangers of data bias, mass surveillance or the construction of autonomous weapons, creates yet more parallels.
So, it doesn’t seem unreasonable to conclude that we could be on the brink of a truly revolutionary moment in history, equal to other industrial revolutions.
Not everyone agrees, though. Let’s take a look at some of their reasons for being skeptical.
Revolution Or Evolution?
Critics of the fourth revolution theory point out that, in many ways, the development of AI and automation is really just an evolution and convergence of previous breakthrough technologies.
AI is, after all, built around digital technology and has fundamentally become possible due to the huge increases in available computing power and the widespread digitization of data prompted by the third industrial revolution.
There’s also the fact that in its current state, most AI applications are highly specialized, only capable of carrying out a narrow range of tasks. This is in contrast to breakthroughs such as the steam engine, electricity and computing, which immediately had wide applications throughout industry and society.
It can be argued that recent developments in AI, such as the large language models (LLMs) powering tools like ChatGPT, which are technically capable of many different language-related tasks, represent steps towards broader AI that can be applied to many tasks. But true, general AI is still considered to be a future goal.
Another factor that can’t be overlooked is the environmental impact. The mechanical revolution – fueled by oil and coal – clearly had a substantial impact on the natural world. However, our understanding of the damage being done at the time was severely limited compared to now.
The energy inefficiency and carbon output created by AI data centers, on the other hand, can easily be quantified today. And the results are certainly a cause for concern. While progress has been made to transition to clean energy sources and achieve net zero emission targets, it remains to be seen whether this will be an obstacle that will prevent AI from becoming truly revolutionary.
The Path Of Progress
Despite these challenges, my personal belief is that AI has the potential to change the world as dramatically as the groundbreaking technologies that sparked previous industrial revolutions.
Whether or not it lives up to that potential, however, depends on how we manage the many ethical, societal and technological challenges that it brings to the table.
Remember that the changes brought about by mechanization, electrification and digitization didn’t happen overnight. Decades passed between the discoveries of Franklin and Faraday and the integration of electricity into everyday life by the likes of Edison and Tesla. The same was true of the transition of Babbage and Turing’s early “counting machines” into the machines marketed by IBM and Apple in the late twentieth century.
Eventually, however, as barriers are broken and challenges are solved, I believe we will come to see the emergence of AI as a pivotal technological breakthrough in line with previous industrial revolutions.
Some - like Google CEO Sundar Pichai – believe it may be even more significant – he famously said it will be even more transformational than fire.
So, while there’s certainly a great deal of hype around the topic of the fourth industrial revolution and the changes it will bring, I think it would be foolish to simply dismiss it as hot air. The AI revolution is only just getting underway, and in the coming years, we’re likely to see it change our world in some pretty amazing ways.

title: Council Post: 6 Terms You Must Know To Navigate The AI Industry
text:
Gaurav Aggarwal is Co-Founder of Truva, helping SaaS businesses improve customer adoption and reduce churn with AI, and a Forbes U30 honoree
LLM this, LLM that. Everywhere I go, I see it. The generative AI space is buzzing with lots of words and technical jargon flying around—be it in casual conversations or mixer events. I think it's best to have a good understanding of some of these words so that when there’s a mention of them, you are at the top of your game regarding what the discussion is all about.
Let's take a look at the terms you should know if you’re looking to get into the generative AI space.
Large Language Models (LLMs)
These are advanced AI systems designed to understand and generate natural language. They can write text, answer questions and even create content that feels like it was written by a human. LLMs are essentially next-word predictors—for example, "The early bird catches the..."—"...worm." "Worm" would make more sense than, say, a truck, right?
Training A Model
Training a language model is a process that involves many steps. They range from teaching the model to perform specific tasks by using training data, measuring its performance concerning the evaluation parameters and adjusting its internal parameters or weights to improve results.
You might have noticed in the news that with every new version released, AI companies try to beat the benchmarks that have been created. These benchmarks are evaluation measures that the trained model is tested against and how the model ranks on the ever-updating LLM leaderboards. One popular benchmark is MMLU.
Architectures
It is also worthwhile to mention more about architectures and transformers while learning about LLMs without getting into the nitty-gritty of it. Model architecture is the underlying structure of an LLM, which includes the way its algorithms are organized and how they process information.
LLMs are based on transformer architecture, which is the type of model architecture that's particularly good at handling sequences of data, like sentences in a paragraph. You might also have heard about convolutional neural network (CNNs); these are particularly effective with image-based data and applications.
Fine-Tuning
Fine-tuning is the process of adjusting a pre-trained LLM on a smaller, specific dataset to specialize it for a particular task or knowledge domain. In this process, the weights (internal parameters) of the initial model are updated, and this is how it becomes good at understanding and generating language that is clear to the domain. Although very fruitful, this is a highly expensive and resource-intensive process.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG)
RAG extends the already powerful capabilities of LLMs to specific domains or an organization's internal knowledge base, all without the need to retrain the model. This makes it more cost-effective. This technique essentially does real-time addition of contextual knowledge with the users' query input.
Let’s take a look at the three-step process of how RAG works.
When a query or input is received, the RAG model uses the retrieval mechanism to search through a predefined corpus or a database to find relevant documents or passages. Vector databases are a popular choice to serve this particular function. This is done using a retrieval model such as Okapi BM25 (BM stands for best-match), dense embeddings or other search algorithms.
Then, the retrieved documents provide additional context to help the generative model formulate a response. This step involves encoding the retrieved passages and converting the tokens (input) into vectors, which are numerical representations of the tokens that also capture their semantic meaning and similarity. Encoder models like BERT take into account the context in which words appear, not just their individual meanings.
If we take an example of a sentence: "He took a loan from the bank." The word "bank" in this context means a financial institution. Now take another sentence: "He sat on the river bank." Here, "bank" refers to the side of a river. The encoder model will produce a different vector for "bank" in both these contexts. These vectors or numbers, despite being the same word, have different meanings and so will be different in their numerical value.
The third step involves the integration of the encoded documents with the query in a way that the generative model can integrate the retrieved information. This involves mechanisms like attention layers in the case of the transformer models. Finally, the combined context (query + retrieved documents) is fed into the generative model. The generation process benefits from the combination of external knowledge provided by the retrieval step and the intent expressed in the query by the user, leading to more accurate and informative outputs.
Vector Databases
There was a mention of vector databases in the previous section. It’s worthwhile to know about these databases as they will be an important part when building GenAI products. As the name suggests, these databases store the numerical representations of data. So why don’t the traditional databases suit vectors?
Traditional scalar-based databases face several pain points with vector data. Vector data involves multiple dimensions, making operations more complex than single-value scalar data. In the case of vectors, there is reliance on similarity searches, such as finding the nearest neighbors in a high-dimensional space instead of exact indexing. These operations are computationally intensive and not well-supported by scalar-based databases.
Final Thoughts
This article serves as an introduction to some specific, important terms that are used when building AI products. For the scope of simplification and more generalization, there is less use of jargon to explain; hence, this may decrease the accuracy of the explanations as well. There are many more terms to cover, but this article provides a primer on the main technical terms you'll encounter as you navigate the AI space.

title: Council Post: AI Hallucinations: How Can Businesses Mitigate Their Impact?
text:
Steve Taplin is the CEO and cofounder of Sonatafy Technology, providing experienced nearshore software developers and engineers.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized numerous industries, offering unprecedented data analysis, customer service and decision-making capabilities. However, like any powerful tool, AI comes with challenges.
One more intriguing and potentially disruptive phenomenon is the “AI hallucination.” This occurs when an AI system generates outputs or makes predictions not grounded in the input data or reality. As companies increasingly depend on AI, recognizing and addressing AI hallucinations becomes critical to maintaining trust, accuracy and efficiency.
What Are AI Hallucinations?
AI hallucinations are particularly prevalent in natural language processing (NLP) models, such as GPT-3, where the AI produces responses that seem coherent and plausible but are factually incorrect or nonsensical. These hallucinations can stem from several factors, including data quality, model limitations and the inherent nature of AI systems, which lack proper understanding and rely solely on pattern recognition.
How Do AI Hallucinations Affect Business?
As CEO of a global software development company, I have seen firsthand how AI hallucinations can affect business operations. Here are some key areas where these issues manifest and the potential consequences:
1. Misinformation: AI-driven content creation and customer service tools enhance efficiency and engagement. However, when these systems hallucinate, they can spread misinformation. For instance, if an AI-powered chatbot provides incorrect answers to customer inquiries, it can damage the company's reputation and erode customer trust.
2. Decision-Making Risks: Businesses increasingly rely on AI for data-driven decision-making. If AI systems hallucinate, they can generate flawed insights, leading to poor strategic choices. For example, a financial institution using AI to predict market trends could make misguided investments based on incorrect data, resulting in significant financial losses.
3. Customer Experience: AI hallucinations can degrade the customer experience. Imagine a scenario where an AI assistant suggests a nonexistent feature of a product or misinterprets a customer's needs. Such errors frustrate customers and reflect poorly on the brand's reliability.
4. Compliance And Legal Issues: Accurate information is paramount in regulated industries. AI hallucinations can lead to noncompliance with legal standards, exposing companies to fines and legal challenges. For instance, healthcare providers using AI to assist in diagnosing patients must ensure that the information provided is accurate and reliable.
Case Studies
Over the past 12 months, my company has encountered and addressed AI hallucinations in various projects. Here are a couple of examples:
1. Customer Service Enhancement: We implemented an AI-powered chatbot for an e-commerce client. Initially, the chatbot occasionally generated incorrect responses about product specifications. To mitigate this, we introduced a human-in-the-loop system where human agents would verify the AI's responses before they were sent to customers. This approach reduced misinformation and improved the chatbot's learning over time.
2. Predictive Analytics In Marketing: For a marketing client, our AI system was designed to predict consumer trends based on social media data. However, AI sometimes hallucinates trends that are not supported by the actual data. By continuously monitoring the AI's outputs and cross-referencing them with human insights, we fine-tuned the model, enhancing its accuracy and reliability.
Mitigating AI Hallucinations
Here are some strategies that my company has used to mitigate the impact of AI hallucinations:
1. Robust Training Data: It is crucial to ensure high-quality, diverse and unbiased training data. AI systems learn from the data they are fed, so any inaccuracies or biases in the data can lead to hallucinations. Regularly updating the training data with new, relevant information can help maintain the AI's accuracy.
2. Human-In-The-Loop: Incorporating human oversight in AI systems is an effective way to catch and correct errors. At Sonatafy, we have found that involving human experts to verify AI outputs reduces hallucinations and enhances the AI's learning and performance over time.
3. Continuous Monitoring And Updating: AI systems should not be set and forgotten. Continuous monitoring of AI outputs and regular updates to the model are essential to ensure it remains accurate and relevant. This involves tracking the AI's performance, identifying hallucination patterns and making necessary adjustments.
4. Clear Communication: Transparency is critical when dealing with AI systems. Businesses should clearly communicate the limitations of AI to users and stakeholders. This helps manage expectations and ensures that any outputs are interpreted with the appropriate level of scrutiny.
5. Multi-Model Approaches: Using multiple AI models and cross verifying their outputs can help identify and mitigate hallucinations. This approach leverages the strengths of different models, reducing the likelihood of errors and enhancing overall accuracy.
The Road Ahead
AI hallucinations pose significant risks, but businesses can effectively navigate these challenges with the right strategies. At my company, we continue to refine our approaches to ensure that our AI systems deliver accurate, reliable and valuable outputs. By understanding the root causes of AI hallucinations and implementing robust mitigation strategies, businesses can harness the full potential of AI while minimizing the associated risks.
As we move forward, it is essential for businesses to stay informed about the latest developments in AI and be proactive in addressing any challenges that arise. By committing to transparency, continuous improvement and collaboration, we can turn AI's promise into a reality that benefits everyone.
