title: Council Post: Building Trust In AI: Ethical Practices For Technology Companies
text:
Dmitry Sokolowski, founder and CTO of Volt AI.
2024 is the year when businesses across industries are learning how to adopt artificial intelligence (AI) into their operations and partnering with AI companies that can assist with these needs. Local governments, schools and law enforcement, for example, are looking into how to keep people safer by using technology in security cameras. Businesses, in turn, are using AI for customer relationship management, cybersecurity and content production, with most business owners believing AI will benefit their businesses.
There are many positive impacts of using AI in business. With the launch of ChatGPT last year, workers are already using the tool to generate content quickly and create personalized experiences for customers. Knowledge workers are also learning to use GenAI to draw insights from unstructured data (like large amounts of text) and reorganize how they perform their jobs by using AI to automate mundane, repetitive tasks, leaving more time to optimize outcomes where human interaction and communication are key. It’s clear that organizations are using AI to their advantage now more than ever before.
People Are Concerned About AI
Despite the positive image of AI among business owners, the 2024 Edelman Trust Barometer Key Insights Around AI Report shows how societal trust in AI companies has declined since 2019 with resistance to the adoption of AI being stronger in developed markets like France, Canada and the U.S. The reason for this resistance is centered around concerns about AI’s potential harm to society and compromises on privacy.
In the United States alone, 52% of Americans are more concerned than excited about AI in daily life, and many are concerned about the negative impact on jobs—for example, 83% of Americans think driverless cars would lead to job loss for ride-share and delivery drivers. A majority of Americans also believe that as companies begin to use AI on a regular basis, personal information will be used in unintended ways that people are not comfortable with.
As the CTO of Volt AI with over 10 years of engineering and software leadership experience at Meta, Uber, Amazon and Apple, I take these concerns about AI seriously. It is incumbent on leaders at AI companies, particularly in the security industry, to address these concerns, explain the benefits of AI to individuals and implement ethical technology practices in business operations.
Let's take a look at three development practices tech companies should embrace in light of this.
1. Demonstrate Transparency And Privacy Protection
Companies should clearly communicate how they collect, use and store data to all of their stakeholders and build robust mechanisms for accountability. For example, The American Institute of CPAs (AICPA) has created a rigorous auditing procedure for service providers storing customer data in the cloud. When a service provider seeks to obtain System and Organization Control Compliance (SOC Compliance) through the AICPA, it shows a commitment to building trust, mitigating risk and safeguarding customer data against unauthorized access.
2. Engage Human-In-The-Loop Approaches For Robust Technology
It is critical to involve human judgment in AI applications and to have humans conduct extensive testing to ensure AI systems operate safely and predictably in various environments and conditions. Having humans in charge of the development and implementation of AI applications ensures another level of testing for accuracy and correction against bias. Adhering to human-in-the-loop guards against significant job loss in an organization, ensuring AI augments rather than replaces human judgment.
3. Practice Fairness And Implement Non-Discrimination Policies
Organizations can develop and enforce comprehensive ethical guidelines for AI development and deployment. For example, companies should implement rigorous testing to specifically identify and eliminate biases in AI models to ensure fairness across diverse demographic groups before their product goes to market and thereafter. Organizations should also include and engage cross-functional, diverse teams in the AI development process to incorporate multiple perspectives. Google AI, for example, published general recommended practices for AI, while IBM’s AI Fairness 360 makes available an open-source toolkit to examine, report and mitigate bias in machine learning models for AI applications.
Conclusion
While we continue to create AI models and adopt them into our workflows, AI companies need to address public concerns with clear communication, transparency and a demonstrated commitment to privacy protection. While we use technology to make a positive impact in the world, we should remember that technology serves people, and we have a responsibility to develop it ethically.

title: Through The Looking Glass: AI Lessons From The Web3 Boom,Bust And Boom
text:
The artificial intelligence sector is experiencing an unprecedented surge in investment, reminiscent of the Web3 and cryptocurrency boom of recent years. With investments by Nvidia, AWS, Google, OpenAI, and more startups entering everyday, how do investors, technologists, and business leaders know where to place their focus.
The global AI market is experiencing remarkable growth, with investments surging to new heights. Per Grand View Research, the market is projected to reach approximately $184 billion, which is staggering. In the U.S. alone, the AI market is anticipated to expand from $55.8 billion this year to a whopping $219 billion by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 25.6%. This tells me that there's a significant momentum driving this sector forward.
When we look at the broader landscape, I think it's fascinating to see that, per IngestAI, the U.S. has led the way with around $290 billion in venture capital investments in AI over the past five years. This number, in my view, underscores just how crucial AI has become to tech giants, startups, and research institutions alike. But it's not just the U.S. that's making waves. China is expected to push its AI market beyond $61 billion by 2025, which I find quite impressive, given their strong state-driven growth strategy.
In my opinion, these figures highlight the massive scale and the broad applicability of AI across different sectors, from healthcare to autonomous systems. This is not just a trend; it's a transformation that's shaping our future in profound ways
Both web3 and AI waves captured the imagination of investors, promising revolutionary changes to technology and society. However, as the dust settles on the Web3 boom and bust and boom cycles, investors, technologists, and business leaders in AI would do well to heed the lessons learned. I’ve been exploring the parallels between these two transformative technologies and their respective landscapes.
The Hype Cycle: Web3 vs. AI
Both Web3 and AI experienced similar patterns of hype and excitement in their early stages. Media coverage played a significant role in fueling public interest and investment in both sectors, much of it accurate and insightful but inevitably, some of it quite wide of the mark. However, the more tangible and immediately applicable use cases of AI have captured the public imagination to a significantly greater degree than the often abstract promises of Web3.
This has significant implications for investors, who must discern between genuine potential and overblown expectations in both cases. They must also learn to identify those who claim AI will bring armageddon and those who claim it represents no challenges to humanity at all – and treat these two imposters just the same.
The fact that AI is dominating the front pages (and not just in the tech press) suggests that the scale of investment will outstrip that experienced even by crypto. While both peak periods (crypto in 2021 and AI in 2023) are comparable, with both sectors attracting tens of billions of dollars in venture capital, the AI sector, particularly generative AI, might have seen even more aggressive funding rounds in a shorter period due to its perceived broader applicability across industries.
I was speaking with Cathy Hackl, a tech and gaming executive and co-founder of a stealth startup this weekend. She said that she believes that "AI and Web3 are not just buzzwords; they're transformative technologies with the potential to reshape our digital landscape. For investors, the key is to look beyond the hype and focus on projects solving real-world problems with clear use cases. Remember, we're in this for the long haul - both AI and Web3 will take years to fully mature and realize their potential. It's not just about investing in tech, but in the vision of a more efficient, equitable, and innovative future."
It’s not just about the numbers, either: the focus of investment is different. Crypto investments were largely driven by speculative trading, decentralized finance (DeFi), and the emergence of non-fungible tokens (NFTs). In contrast, AI investments are more diversified, spanning across enterprise applications, consumer products, and foundational research, indicating a broader potential impact.
The Patterns
Early adopters and tech enthusiasts were the first to jump into both Web3 and AI investments. As buzz grew, institutional investors began to take notice, lending credibility and injecting significant capital into both sectors. The influx of retail investors followed, often driven by fear of missing out (FOMO) and the promise of quick returns. Venture capital played a crucial role in both ecosystems, funding startups and fueling innovation at a rapid pace.
Web3 promised a decentralized internet, while AI offers the potential for unprecedented automation and intelligence in various domains. Both technologies faced challenges in delivering on their ambitious claims, with Web3 struggling with scalability and user adoption, and AI grappling with issues of bias, reliability and data security. The gap between technological promises and real-world implementation has been a sobering reality for investors in both sectors.
Market Correction and Consolidation
The Web3 and crypto markets experienced a significant crash, leading to a period of consolidation and reassessment. That’s hardly surprising, given that they are based on digital tokens which, like any asset with a market value, can be highly volatile. While the AI market is more insulated from the speculator-driven ‘valuation rollercoaster’ and consequently hasn't seen a comparable crash, there are signs of potential correction as the initial euphoria gives way to more realistic expectations. Investors are becoming more discerning, focusing on AI companies with solid business models and clear paths to profitability.
Regulation played a significant role in shaping the Web3 and crypto investment landscape, with unclear guidelines and crackdowns causing market volatility. The AI sector is now facing increasing scrutiny from regulators concerned about privacy, bias, and the societal impact of the technology. Investors in AI must be prepared for a shifting regulatory landscape that could significantly impact the sector's growth and direction.
In the aftermath of the Web3 boom, it became clear that some projects offered genuine innovation while others were purely speculative. Similarly, the AI sector is seeing a mix of truly groundbreaking applications and overhyped solutions. Technologists, investors, and users are challenged to distinguish between AI companies offering sustainable value and those riding the wave of speculative enthusiasm.
Lessons for AI
The AI clock started ticking decades ago, with steady progress in machine learning and neural networks laying the groundwork for today's breakthroughs. In fact, significant AI investment predates the crypto and Web3 boom. As someone who began working in AI back in 2013, I've witnessed firsthand the long-term development and investment cycles in this field.
OpenAI's ChatGPT represents AI's "Netscape moment," catalyzing widespread adoption and sparking a new wave of innovation.
In fact on X (Twitter), Blitzscaling Ventures general partner Jeremiah Owyang commented that “AI agents will autonomously handle laborious tasks for us, such as managing repetitive emails, filling out expense reports, booking travel, scheduling calls, doing internet research, and performing monotonous e-commerce tasks. It won’t be perfect, it will take time to refine.As a result, information will come to humans in just a few user interfaces where we can manage our agent workers, reducing the need to traverse websites.
In contrast, blockchain technology, though younger, is rapidly evolving to address both consumer and enterprise needs. Its decentralized nature introduces unique complexities, but also promises revolutionary applications across various sectors.
The Web3 experience underscores the importance of thorough due diligence and a deep understanding of the underlying technology. AI investors should heed these lessons, being wary of unrealistic promises and focusing on companies with clear use cases and revenue models. Maintaining a long-term perspective is crucial, as the full potential of AI, like Web3, may take years to materialize fully.
As these technologies mature, we're likely to see a convergence, with AI enhancing blockchain capabilities and decentralized systems providing new frameworks for AI deployment and governance. The key for investors and innovators alike is to balance enthusiasm with realistic expectations, recognizing that true technological revolutions often unfold over decades rather than months.
With AI reaching into almost every aspect of life, the future will almost certainly see an integration of AI and Web3 technologies, creating new opportunities as this intersection acts as a “force multiplier” for each revolution’s transformative capabilities. Decentralized AI systems and blockchain-based machine learning marketplaces are just a few potential areas of convergence. So, for investors it’s not a case of either/or: they need to keep an eye on the evolving, often symbiotic landscapes of both Web3 and AI, the implications of new developments on each other, and on the wider tech and industry investment landscapes.
The AI investment boom shares many similarities with the Web3 cycle, but also presents unique opportunities and challenges. By learning from the Web3 experience, investors can navigate the AI landscape more wisely, balancing enthusiasm with caution. Ultimately, both AI and Web3 represent transformative technologies that will continue to shape our digital future, regardless of short-term investment trends.
Emphasize Regulatory Awareness and Ethical Considerations
As with Web3, the AI industry is poised to encounter significant regulatory scrutiny. The implications of AI on privacy, bias, and ethical standards are already drawing the attention of regulators worldwide.
For AI investors, it is crucial to consider the regulatory landscape and invest in companies that not only comply with current laws but are also proactive in addressing potential future regulations. Companies that prioritize ethical AI development, ensuring transparency, fairness, and accountability, are more likely to sustain long-term success and public trust.
It’s All About the Business
As we navigate the exciting yet complex landscapes of AI and Web3, investors, technologists, and business leaders must approach these fields with both enthusiasm and caution. Choose your investments and projects carefully, looking beyond flashy demos to examine the underlying data strategy – it's the fuel that powers these technologies.
Pay close attention to change management; the most brilliant innovation is worthless if your team or customers can't adapt to it. Keep a laser focus on tangible business outcomes rather than getting lost in technological rabbit holes. Remember, success in these domains often comes from starting small: begin with pilot projects that demonstrate clear value and build from there.
By taking measured steps, learning from each iteration, and staying aligned with core business objectives, you'll be better positioned to harness the transformative potential of AI and Web3 while mitigating risks. In this rapidly evolving landscape, those who combine visionary thinking with pragmatic execution will be the ones who truly thrive.

title: Council Post: 15 Important Ways AI-Human Hybrid Coaching Models Can Help Coaches
text:
For professional coaches, using an AI-human hybrid model integrates the strengths of artificial intelligence with invaluable human coaching expertise. Such collaborative models can help coaches achieve better results more efficiently by helping to analyze vast amounts of data, quickly identifying patterns in behaviors, predicting the best course of action for the best outcomes, developing personalized content and experiences to better guide clients and much more.
Below, 15 members of Forbes Coaches Council share applications of AI that they are particularly excited about or that have already benefited their coaching practice. Read on to learn how adopting AI tools and resources for their practice’s most relevant and impactful use cases can allow a coach to execute more tailored and effective engagements in shorter amounts of time.

As someone who provides interview preparation, I find it exciting how AI can construct potential interview questions that match the job description and help clients tailor their elevator pitch to highlight key elements from their experience that match the potential job. I find it very useful in assisting candidates to prepare for upcoming interviews. - Jasmine Briggs-Rogers, Creatively Inspired Career Coaching

I use AI to identify gaps during “mock interview sessions” with a client, and quickly add my own expertise to those areas of improvement to provide strong feedback to the candidate. - Astika Gupta, The Product Seat

AI could enable a coach to make timely adjustments to the coaching plan that a client can put into immediate practice. - Curtis Odom, Prescient Strategists

An AI-human hybrid coaching model can offer personalized, data-driven insights and feedback, allowing coaches to tailor sessions more effectively. This model can analyze client progress patterns and suggest evidence-based strategies, enhancing coaching efficacy and enabling more precise support, which ultimately benefits both coach and client. - Adaora Ayoade, EZ37 Solutions

title: Council Post: 16 Predictions About AI, Content Creation And Its Effect On Business
text:
Generative AI and other AI-powered tools have permeated the workplace in a short time, and they show no signs of slowing down. With new innovations and use cases popping up every day, the world is left wondering what impact AI will have on their jobs and the future of content creation.
As experts in the marketing and communications field, the leaders of Forbes Communications Council have first-hand experience with generative AI and its capabilities. Here, they weigh in with their predictions about the future of AI-powered content creation and its effect on businesses and consumers alike.
1. AI Will Enhance The Efficiency Of Persona-Optimized Content Distribution
I believe that AI, when provided with properly vetted data and human oversight, will enhance efficiencies in distributing persona-optimized content across all stages of the identified buyer journey. This will allow for greater focus on content strategy related to topical or unique subject matter, ultimately leading to an improved overall customer experience. - Stephen Spratley, Marketing Armor
2. It Will Create More Jobs And Opportunities
AI content is going to create more jobs and opportunities than it is going to eliminate. It's essentially leveled-up automation or a really good intern; it's not going to replace the need for actual humans to produce effective content. As we are able to create more content at scale, good content will continue to rise to the top—and that will require human oversight, every time. - Ellen Sluder, smrtPhone
3. It Will Evolve Into Fully Autonomous Marketing Ecosystems
AI-powered content will evolve into fully autonomous marketing ecosystems, generating, optimizing and deploying content across multiple channels in real time. Leveraging vast data to predict consumer behavior with high precision, it will adapt instantaneously to market changes and preferences. This will lead to highly effective marketing, freeing human talent for strategic innovation. - Sandra Marchand, Advanced Technology Services
4. It Will Democratize And Break Barriers Around Content Creation
Generative AI will democratize content creation. Translating knowledge into content becomes a lot easier. The format of content sharing will go through an evolution. Multimodal content will become the norm. For businesses, real original knowledge becomes the differentiator. Once the barrier on content creation goes away, this will lead to a lot more content, and original content will stand out. - Saravana Sivanandham, Absorb Software
5. It Will Enhance Creativity Without Exhausting Resources
AI-powered content creation will continue to enhance creativity, allowing for high-quality content without exhausting resources and enabling organizations to amplify diverse voices and foster innovation. As AI tools advance, they will benefit businesses and consumers with richer, more diverse content experiences and outcomes in the digital landscape. - Jonathan Kaufman, Sage Dental

6. It Will Improve Content Accessibility
I predict we’ll see more brands leverage generative AI to improve accessibility. Not only is accessibility good for inclusivity, but it also allows brands to reach a broader audience. On the social media front, for example, marketers are using new AI-powered content creation tools to produce alt text for social post images, which enhances social accessibility and saves marketing teams time. - Scott Morris, Sprout Social
7. It Will Allow For A Deeper Understanding Of Your Audience
The key to effective content creation is knowing your customer. This is tough because many content creators rely on sales for indirect insights. AI has enabled a new type of research based on synthetic customers trained to mimic buyer personas. Imagine creating content based on digital conversations with these AI customers! 8. It Will Help Brands Produce Interactive And Immersive Experiences
If a picture speaks a thousand words, AI will amplify this to a million through the seamless fusion of voice and visual content generation. As AI technology advances, businesses will be able to produce interactive and immersive content experiences. This will revolutionize how businesses communicate with consumers, leading to more dynamic and compelling brand experiences. - Resha Chheda, Safe Security
9. It Will Raise the Bar For Social Media Content
I expect AI to increase the quality and quantity of social media content, raising the bar for brands, agencies and creators. AI will also separate the good, the bad and the ugly, with smart social media teams elevating their game and lazy ones overly relying on generative AI and likely being punished by already critical audiences. - Rafael Schwarz, TERRITORY Influence (a Bertelsmann group company)
10. It Will Help Scale Personalized Interactions
AI will revolutionize personalization, enhancing user experiences with hyper-targeted content. Businesses will leverage AI to scale personalized interactions, driving deeper customer engagement and operational efficiencies. - Jorge Lukowski, NEORIS
11. It Will Allow More Human Stories (And Brands) To Stand Out
While AI will enable businesses to produce a lot of content, companies that are creative and spend time producing standout content will rise to the top. Producing content that involves human stories, includes more detail than AI-generated content, involves multiple types of media or has a creative angle will beat the AI-generated content in search, social and with actual humans. - Tom Treanor, Snipp Interactive
12. It Will Drive A Need For More Human-To-Human Engagement
Using AI to personalize the customer experience will be the most effective way to scale, but organizations need to first ensure that the information served to customers is relevant and rooted in trusted organization-specific contextual content. AI will never be able to replicate the empathetic marketing of a human, so AI is useful for specific use cases but not all. Human-to-human engagement is still critical. - Niki Hall, Five9
13. It Will Adapt To Individual Preferences In Real Time
Thanks to AI, most (if not all) digital content will adapt to individual preferences in real time. This is already true in digital advertising. In the future, emails and websites will match your personal communication style, and retailer sites will default to merchandise in your preferred colors and other preferences. Both businesses and consumers will benefit from more relevant content powered by AI. - Stephanie Bunnell, Aki Technologies
14. It Will Help Support Our Planet's Health
I foresee AI-driven content creation prioritizing not just efficiency but also environmental impact. As businesses and consumers grow more eco-conscious, the push for AI tools that minimize energy use and carbon emissions will intensify. This evolution will ensure that AI helps in crafting compelling narratives while also supporting our planet's health—a crucial balance for future innovation. - Brittany Garlin, BDG Alliance
15. It Will Lead To A Surge In Content Volume
AI will continue to reshape how content is created, distributed and consumed. The speed at which content can be created will lead to a surge in volume, so marketers should focus on quality, not quantity. Having a clear strategy for creating and managing AI-powered content is imperative for organizations to stay true to their brands. - Clay Tuten, KeyMark Inc.
16. It Will Need To Be Balanced With Human Ingenuity
As AI advances, so do the use cases within content generation. We're now seeing advertisements offering AI to help consumers write letters. There is a potential risk there: As AI writes more, humans write less, exacerbating the communication decline in our younger, tech-first generation. Striking a balance between AI assistance and human ingenuity is crucial. - Sherri Schwartz, OvationCXM

title: Council Post: GenAI Vs. Robo-Advisors: Considerations For The Financial Industry
text:
Tamara Kostova, CEO of Velexa, empowers institutional clients through customized and embedded investing services.
Many companies were quick to append the acronym “AI” to any and every service remotely related to artificial intelligence after OpenAI’s public launch of ChatGPT at the end of 2022. Suddenly, these services were incorrectly being called “AI” in an effort to jump on the bandwagon.
The frenzy prompted the Federal Trade Commission to issue a stern warning in February 2023 about labeling products as “AI” when they weren’t. The FTC ended the warning with the tongue-in-cheek statement, “You don’t need a machine to predict what the FTC might do when those claims are unsupported.”
Being the CEO of an investing platform, I believe the concerns raised about generative AI—such as privacy concerns, copyright infringement and inherent biases—are quite legitimate. The financial sector has been using a form of AI since the 1980s to help with investing, financial planning and more. In 2008, the first consumer-facing robo-advisors were launched. But to confuse this mathematical technology with GenAI is misguided.
Robo-advisory isn’t the same as generative AI.
GenAI is a different application of AI technology than the mathematical models and machine learning algorithms that financial institutions have been using in robo-advisory. Both technologies can be called “AI,” just as an orange and a banana can both be called a “fruit.” But, internally, GenAI and the AI used for robo-advisory are different.
To get into the precise details of how GenAI differs from robo-advisory on a technical level would require a book, but from a high-level view, robo-advisor algorithms have been designed to follow investment best practices, and they typically follow a passive-indexing strategy. However, different robo-advisors will implement different proprietary algorithms.
GenAI like ChatGPT uses large language models. LLMs tend to struggle with mathematical computations, as they aren’t primarily designed to perform mathematical operations. Instead, GenAI is intended for generative functions, such as generating contextually relevant responses to user prompts. LLMs work through something called neural networks. These neural networks remain somewhat of a black box to designers. AI has also been found to hallucinate and produce erroneous outputs.
That said, robo-advisors also aren’t always right, just as financial advisors aren’t always right. From my observations, the errors of robo-advisory typically come down to incorrect algorithms and the inherent unpredictability of financial markets, despite our best efforts to attempt to predict them. Statistics predict probable outcomes, never guaranteed ones.
By lumping robo-advisory technology with GenAI, I believe we risk closing the door on underserved investors for whom robo-advisory opened the door in the first place.
Exactly how generative AI is used in robo-advising matters.
Still, GenAI has its use. Coupled with existing, mathematically precise robo-advisory AI, many powerful tools become possible.
For example, Morgan Stanley was the first major financial player to announce an OpenAI-integrated chatbot for use in financial advising. The bot was created for the company's financial advisors and their support staff. It will provide advisors with "access to a database of about 100,000 research reports and documents," CNBC said.
JPMorgan’s GenAI-powered robo-advisor is more ambitious. The financial services giant has registered a trademark called IndexGPT and plans to release its bot directly to consumers.
Given the financial sector’s heavy regulatory ecosystem, clearly demarcated guardrails and the reputation of these two companies, it’s hard to imagine that any GenAI implementation would be done in such a way as to bring them legal battles in the future. Presumably, both these tools will either have extremely clear warnings on them or they’ll be programmed to augment, rather than replace, existing, functioning AI technology.
From my perspective, the same is not necessarily true about startups that are hungry for market share, especially given the challenges robo-advisor startups have faced when trying to disrupt the industry. Some of those startups might consider GenAI the silver bullet they’ve been waiting for to give them an edge over incumbents. In this sense, yes, regulation might be welcome, but where does the line for regulation vs. innovation in AI begin and end?
Robo-advisors helped open the door to an underserved sector.
Robo-advisors opened the door to an underserved sector of investors who did have some capital to invest but not enough to purchase professional advisory services. Collectively, that capital is immense and a much-needed source of revenue for larger funds seeking to make their revenue targets. Catering to this demographic individually would be impossible. I believe intelligently developed and responsibly implemented robo-advisory software can keep this demographic active in investing.
The other door opener is intelligent regulations. Grouping all robo-advisory services into a lump, whether they use GenAI or not, would be the biggest mistake. As I see it, doing so could stifle an industry that has been running successfully without using GenAI. Some professionals in the tech industry have said the European Union's AI Act, for example, is too broad and "may catch forms of AI that are harmless."
That's a challenge. AI companies need to ensure regulators understand these nuances. Leaders can do so through joining trade bodies, putting out educational materials and inviting regulators to be part of roundtables or panels.
It's also essential that those of us in the financial sector are critical when assessing AI-enabled partners. In addition to their feature set, it is important to investigate the fundamental technology and the types of strategies implemented for end users. This will also tie into the longer development of AI and what future strategies it could potentially implement. Another consideration is data privacy and security, as there is much sensitive financial information to be ingested.
AI is not just a black box we as leaders should simply accept for use; instead, it should be scrutinized and selected carefully, just like any other technology provider.

title: Council Post: Get Your Edge With AI: Three Tips For E-Commerce SMBs
text:
As founder and CEO of Webgility, Parag Mamnani builds software that boosts success for small businesses in retail and e-commerce.
Over the past few years, there has been endless speculation about the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to transform all types of businesses. The e-commerce sector is no exception—massive global retailers and platforms like Amazon, Shopify and others have been utilizing AI to better understand customer behavior, identify new sales opportunities, improve business operations and more.
The big guys are in a good position to take full advantage of AI because they have tons of data, engineering prowess and scale. Most small and midsize businesses (SMBs), on the other hand, barely have their data organized and captured in one place, let alone have the knowledge or resources to utilize cutting-edge AI-powered predictive models.
But AI is no longer in the distant future for SMBs—it's already here and it's time to act. According to a recent report from McKinsey, 65% of organizations are regularly using generative AI, nearly double the percentage from the previous 2023 survey. SMBs must adapt or risk falling further and further behind.
The issue is less about whether SMBs like AI (because it’s happening, regardless of whether they want it or not) and more about how to stay competitive in an environment that’s dominated by big technology and massive players. The challenge is immediate, and the stakes have never been higher.
So, how can SMBs start utilizing AI to sharpen their competitive edge?
What AI Can And Cannot Do
Before we talk about concrete tips, it’s important to clarify that AI is not a crystal ball that can predict the future, nor is it a magic bullet that will enable SMB owners to forget the fundamentals. For SMBs to reap the benefits of AI, they need to first embrace data, embrace a new way of interacting with software and open their minds to what's possible.
Silicon Valley pundits like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman are predicting the emergence of a new wave of one-person, billion-dollar unicorn companies due to advancements in AI technology. The idea that a business could actually grow faster without hiring more employees may be intriguing, but I believe these will be the outliers, not the norm. For most companies, people are still the core of a business, and technology is there to support, not replace them.
That said, AI can accelerate the way businesses interface with their data. It can also play a critical role by helping to automate processes.
Most small businesses waste countless hours on manual, repetitive tasks. They often use siloed spreadsheets to store their data, which results in weak, error-filled financial reporting that is usually out of date. Many small business owners can’t afford to pay a financial analyst and struggle to find the time to handle accounting processes while simultaneously running their businesses. All of this has an adverse impact on inventory, sales tax compliance and other aspects of business operations which ultimately impacts growth.
Time is the most valuable resource that small businesses have, and AI tools can automate and help to shortcut manual work. This will not only help give time back, but it will also boost margins and improve profitability.
When coupled with accurate data, AI can help SMBs optimize their operations and obtain new insights about how to manage operational costs, inventory, performance data, fulfillment/logistics, gain a better understanding of customers and more.
Three Ways To Leverage AI
Most small business owners are still very new to AI, and many are uncertain as to how it can help them. Here are three tips for getting started:
1. Capture and analyze data. Start by capturing and aggregating all of your data in a centralized place. Most small businesses have tons of data scattered everywhere in lots of different formats. AI tools today have the power to process all kinds of data, structured and unstructured, and they can go through large amounts of data in a short time. You can then summarize and analyze this data with ease.
2. Automate, automate, automate. Identify tasks you're doing manually and look for ways to cut steps or fully automate. Copyrighting, summarizing and researching are just a few areas that can be significantly more efficient with AI. AI-powered tools can save time, improve accuracy, reduce third-party fees and provide better visibility into what’s happening with the business, in real time and with a level of accuracy that far surpasses older technologies.
3. AI + Humans is the answer. AI models are not 100% accurate and you don't want to bank your business entirely on bots. It is always valuable to put new technology in place that addresses pain points for your customers, but even the best technology requires people to support it. Ultimately, most businesses are about supporting customers, so we still need to put people first. The biggest hurdle to the adoption of new technologies is often changing human behaviors and habits, so it’s critical to assess and evaluate what’s out there, engage in some experimentation, establish a timeline for adopting new systems and find sensible ways to enforce it.
AI-powered tools can enable SMB owners to transform the way they operate, rather than struggling with operational details. Ultimately, embracing AI now will enable SMB owners to focus on successfully growing their businesses, faster and in a more efficient way.

title: The Anti-Hiring Manifesto: A Lean Approach To Scaling Your Business
text:
Hiring is the most expensive mistake most businesses make. This might sound like heresy in a world that equates growth with headcount, but hear me out. The traditional model of scaling a business by adding more employees is outdated, inefficient, and often counterproductive.
The Law of Diminishing Returns (With a Twist)
You're likely familiar with the law of diminishing returns in economics: the more of a single input you add, the less additional output you generate. This principle applies perfectly to teams. Initially, adding people boosts productivity. But as your team grows, communication overhead increases, decision-making gets bogged down, and the potential for social loafing rises. Each new hire adds less and less value while the costs keep climbing.
Imagine a simple graph: the x-axis represents the number of employees, and the y-axis represents productivity. The line starts with a steep upward slope, but gradually flattens, and eventually starts to dip downwards. This is the reality of most teams.
The "Drag" of Employees
Think of employees as having a "drag coefficient." This isn't about individual competence, but rather the inherent friction that comes with more people.
Growing a team introduces friction that hinders productivity:
- Communication Overhead: As team size grows, communication overhead increases exponentially, as Frederick Brooks famously noted: “Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.” This principle applies to any project. Brooks’ formula, n(n-1)/2, shows how communication channels multiply rapidly with each new team member. Quick math reveals that 3 people have 3 connections, while 5 people have 10, illustrating the swift rise in complexity.
- Decision-Making Bottlenecks: More people often mean more opinions, longer debates, and slower decisions. Bain & Company reports that decision-making speed drops by 10% for every 10 additional team members.
- Social Loafing: Research from the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology shows that as group size increases, individual effort tends to decrease. People feel less accountable and are more likely to let others pick up the slack.
Calculating your team's drag coefficient is complex, but here's a simplified way to think about it: for every new hire, estimate the additional time spent on communication, meetings, and coordination. Divide that by the expected increase in output. The higher the ratio, the greater the drag.
This is why it's crucial not to underestimate the power of a single, highly motivated individual. Many successful solopreneurs and small businesses have achieved remarkable results with lean teams. They embrace "hyper-productivity," focusing on essential tasks, leveraging technology, and avoiding the distractions and inefficiencies of large groups.
The Tech Trap And The AI Multiplier
Technology can be a double-edged sword. Much of it, like endless software updates and feature-laden platforms, simply adds another layer of complexity and distraction. However, a new breed of tools, powered by artificial intelligence (AI), is fundamentally changing the game.
AI is not just another tool in the junk drawer; it's a force multiplier that can exponentially increase the output of your existing team. AI-powered solutions can automate repetitive tasks, augment human capabilities, and even take on entire job functions.
AI-powered solution worth adopting:
- Content Creation: AI writing tools like ChatGPT can generate marketing copy, social media posts, and even long-form articles with minimal human input.
- Customer Service: Sophisticated chatbots can handle routine inquiries, freeing up human agents to focus on complex issues.
- Data Analysis: AI-powered platforms can sift through massive datasets, uncovering insights and patterns that would take humans weeks or months to find.
- Process Automation: Robotic Process Automation (RPA) can automate repetitive tasks like data entry, invoice processing, and report generation.
Tips for adopting an “Ai-First” mindset
To adopt an "AI-First" mindset, prioritize the exploration of AI tools that align with your business needs. Actively seek out and experiment with these technologies to stay ahead. Invest in training your team to ensure they have the skills necessary to effectively utilize AI tools. Continuously measure the impact of AI on your productivity, and be prepared to adjust your strategy as needed to maximize benefits.
How To Scale Effectively With A Minimum Viable Team Framework
- Define Clear Goals: Set specific, measurable objectives.
- Identify Essential Tasks: Focus on tasks crucial for achieving your goals.
- Map Skills to Tasks: Assess if current team members can be upskilled for these tasks.
- Leverage AI: Explore how AI tools can automate, augment, or even replace certain tasks.
- Hire Strategically: Only add hires for gaps that cannot be filled by existing resources or AI.
Stop Hiring, Start Optimizing
Growth doesn't have to mean a bigger team. Embrace a leaner, more agile approach by optimizing existing resources, and maintaining an "AI-First" mindset. By doing so, you'll not only save money and reduce headaches, but you'll likely achieve better results than you ever imagined. AI is not just the future of work; it's the key to unlocking your business's full potential today.

title: How Morningstar Leads AI Adoption On An Enterprise Scale Level
text:
Morningstar has been collecting, organizing, and disseminating information that powers financial decisions worldwide for forty years. As the volume and complexity of this data has exploded, Morningstar has begun grappling with many of the same vexing challenges occurring in all industries. How do you ingest and harmonize data from a myriad of ever-changing sources? How do you ensure its quality, timeliness, and security of this data in the face of relentless information growth? Perhaps most crucially, how do you translate this sea of numbers and metrics into actionable insights clients can use?
In response, Morningstar's data supply chain has undergone a major transformation by adopting AI to optimize for scale, insights, and explainability.
Within this transformation, Morningstar has embedded its data into the Morningstar Intelligence Engine – a sophisticated platform that enables bespoke generative AI applications. These applications include Morningstar's unstructured data processing in its data collection center, manager research workflows, and Mo. Mo, a Morningstar-branded generative AI chatbot, offers advisors a new way to interface with Morningstar data and is redefining how Morningstar and financial advisors leverage financial information. It provides seamless, comprehensive access to Morningstar's extensive research and data resources, enabling greater operational efficiency, accuracy, and client engagement.
Lee Davidson, Chief Data and Analytics Officer at Morningstar, was the keynote speaker at the Omaxn* event titled Optimizing Data Supply Chains from End-to-End, which took place on July 16, 2024. During the event, he highlighted the company's innovative efforts at optimizing its data supply chain. The event provided an excellent platform to demonstrate Morningstar's strategic commitment to utilizing advanced technologies to transform its data supply chain, integrate AI, and offer exceptional support to financial advisors.
Optimizing the Data Supply Chain: A Transformative Endeavor
Morningstar's meticulous approach to data supply chain management is intertwined with its mission to deliver value to the financial advisory sector. The managed investment industry has continued its torrid pace of innovation, with the total number of managed investment products available for sale globally surpassing one million in 2023, capping off nearly a quarter-century of steady expansion at 8% annual growth. The volume of data on these investments is growing rapidly as well. In 2023, Morningstar ingested more than 130 million documents – a threefold increase over the past five years. During the same five-year period, the number of portfolios ingested more than doubled. The company has tackled the complex challenges of managing this vast and growing data influx through the targeted application of AI and machine learning (ML), enabling it to scale effectively.
One such example is in the area of unstructured data processing, where multiple generative AI agents built from Morningstar's Intelligence Engine are deployed to read and analyze documents and provide recommendations to data analysts based on the key insights and data present in those documents. Increasingly, data analysts at Morningstar can chat with a generative AI agent during the data acquisition process as if it were their own personal assistant to help them gather data. This workflow exemplifies the human-in-the-loop approach that Davidson emphasizes.
Leveraging Generative ML to Scale Research Efforts
The strategic deployment of advanced technologies, including ML, has been instrumental in addressing operational hurdles and enhancing Morningstar's analytics offerings. By incorporating ML techniques into its renowned Medalist Rating system, Morningstar extended its coverage to over 400,000 managed investments globally, providing financial advisors with richer and more comprehensive insights. As a result, the scope of coverage increased tenfold compared to a purely qualitative approach.
The Morningstar Intelligence Engine, which utilizes Azure OpenAI Service in a private, secure environment, is also incorporated into its manager research analysts' workflow through its internal decision support platform. The Intelligence Engine integrates Morningstar's independent research on equities, mutual funds, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), market trends, and financial news and uses advanced ML algorithms and natural language processing (NLP) technologies to deliver precision and accuracy. It also pairs with the analysts' ongoing notes and commentary.
From a workflow perspective, the Intelligence Engine assists manager researchers by turning their interview notes into long-form investment commentary and reformatting first drafts into copy-edited and publication-ready reports. Overall, Davidson estimates that the firm has reduced the per-unit cost of investment strategy analysis by 40% through the thoughtful integration of machine learning and other tools within the Intelligence Engine into its decision-support platform.
Unveiling Mo: Revolutionizing Financial Advisors Engagement
Mo, Morningstar's generative AI chatbot, is at the front end of its data supply chain optimization efforts. Mo represents a significant leap forward for the company as it positions itself at the forefront of AI utilization on an enterprise scale, redefining how financial advisors interact with financial data. Mo's ability to interpret and respond to user queries based on Morningstar's library of investment insights helps advisors receive robust, trusted answers more quickly than ever before.
Davidson notes that the research giant is also exploring methods to provide in-context commentary and talking points for advisors during the investment proposal generation process. By blending Morningstar's extensive investment information with the advisor's capital allocation views and customer metadata, this approach generates a personalized narrative to include in investment proposals.
Davidson commented that the firm intends to continue researching the best ways to reduce friction between advisors' questions of the moment with the insights embedded inside the firm's data content and analytics capabilities.
Morningstar is strategically focused on optimizing its data supply chain and harnessing AI technology through the Morningstar Intelligence Engine. The aim is to set a new standard for advisors' interactions with generative AI applications in the financial services industry. With a relentless focus on the end investor, Morningstar is clearly leading AI innovation in the financial advisory sector.
