title: Pretty Soon, Your Loan Application Will Be Reviewed By A Robot
text:
OBSERVATIONS FROM THE FINTECH SNARK TANK
Efficiency is the name of the game in banking. Itʼs amazing, then—and not in a positive way—that banks' use of lending technology is lacking.
For all the hype in the press about artificial intelligence (AI), just 13% of banks have deployed AI technologies in their credit and lending processes according to a new report from Cornerstone Advisors (commissioned by ZestAI) titled Achieving High-Performance Lending: The Impact of AI on Lending Efficiency.
The Coming Boom In AI-Driven Lending
Despite the low use of AI in lending today, big changes are coming. More than half of the banks surveyed plan to invest $100,000 or more in machine learning-driven credit models over the next three years, with 12% planning to spend $500,000 or more. AI-driven auto-decisioning will increase because of banks’ need for:
- Efficiency. The efficiency gains for automated decisioning are substantial. According to Cornerstone's benchmark data, the number of loan applications reviewed per underwriting FTE per month is 3.5 times greater among banks that use automated decisioning than those that don't.
- Effectiveness. Machine learning models can increase credit access by more accurately identifying applicants who are likely to repay loans and to reduce the number of people given loans that they are unlikely to repay.
AI Brings Familiar Challenges
Skeptics point out that AI will present lenders challenges like:
- Explainability. Understanding how and why a model arrives at a particular decision or prediction can be difficult. Lenders must ensure explainability (i.e., why a model produces the results it does) in their machine learning models to comply with regulatory requirements, address customer inquiries and maintain trust.
- Transparency. The black box nature of many machine learning models has focused attention on model transparency as a critical threshold question for both lenders and regulators.
- Data availability and quality. Accuracy, security, and data availability are challenges with machine learning models. Machine learning models rely on large volumes of high-quality data for training and validation, and banks and credit unions are often challenged to access and aggregate diverse and relevant data sets.
- Model validation and bias mitigation. Models must be thoroughly evaluated to ensure they do not perpetuate biases, discriminate against certain demographics or exhibit unfair behavior. Establishing robust validation processes and addressing bias concerns are essential to ensuring fair and responsible lending practices.
The Benefits of AI-Driven Lending
These aren’t new challenges, however—they’re the same challenges banks face today with manual (i.e., human) loan underwriting. Leveraging machine learning models will help banks:
- Improve credit risk assessment. By incorporating alternative data sources and nonlinear relationships, machine learning models can generate more accurate and comprehensive credit risk assessments, enabling lenders to make more informed lending decisions and better manage risk.
- Create more efficient collections and loss mitigation. Focusing on collections and loss mitigation becomes crucial in a down lending environment. Machine learning models can analyze borrower behavior, payment patterns, and external factors to identify early warning signals of potential delinquency or default.
As Visa concluded in a recent study:
“Lenders that automate decisions were able to auto-decision roughly 50% to 60% of application volume, which drove a more consistent level of decisioning speed and cost reduction while maintaining a stable level of risk performance.”
AI Can Help Ease The Small Business Credit Crisis
AI will do more than just benefit banks—it will help expand minority small business owners’ access to capital. According to the Federal Reserve:
“Black- and Hispanic-owned businesses have a harder time accessing credit from traditional sources because they’re evaluated as higher credit risks. These risks are determined in part by lower owner wealth, lower business revenue, and insufficient credit histories.”
At the heart of the small business fair and accessible solution is data—which is often incorrect, missing or misleading.
According to an analysis from Uplinq, relying strictly on FICO scores for small business loan underwriting can unfairly impact protected class business owners.
The data and technology firm’s analysis found that expanding the set of data inputs used to evaluate protected class small businesses—including data from accounting systems, payment and e-commerce systems, core banking platforms and other sources—could increase the number of good (i.e., non-loss) loans accepted by 215%.
Small business owners’ access to affordable credit can’t be solved by regulatory change. It will improve when the lenders—banks, fintech, and other non-bank lenders—see improved profitability from the use of AI and expanded data sources.

title: Strategic Response Management
text:
Shining a Light on the Unsung Heroes of the Modern Revenue Team
A new study sponsored by the Association of Proposal Management Professionals (APMP) shows that response teams – made up of bid and proposal management professionals – are the “hidden breadwinners” in most B2B organizations. A recent survey of 750 proposal executives and practitioners sponsored by the APMP found that response teams drive almost half of the revenues in a business-to-business organization. Their efforts inform the other half of revenues with customer intelligence, content, knowledge, and accumulated go-to-market “know how.”
But despite the fact that bid and proposal management teams drive the majority of revenues in their businesses, few organizations understand or recognize their large and growing contribution to revenue and profit growth, according to Rick Harris, the CEO of the APMP.
“The APMP is a professional organization that teaches bid and proposal management professionals how to win more business,” says Harris. “Our members are the professionals and executives who write revenue generating proposals and respond to Requests for Information (RFIs), Due Diligence Questionnaires, Requests for Proposals (RFPs), and a wide array of other inquiries from prospects and customers.”
“Every B2B organization has a response function in some form,” Harris continues. “A typical response, bid and proposal team includes an average of eight members according to our (APMP) benchmarks. But response teams can be much larger, as in the case of Microsoft who has a centralized proposal response center of excellence that ‘follows the sun’ and supports over 17,000 stakeholders involved in responding to bids and generating proposals around the globe.”
“Our members are the growth engines of their businesses because they control the growth assets and processes that drive revenues,” says Harris. “They manage a large and growing ecosystem of dozens, or even hundreds, of subject matter experts and customer facing employees involved in generating proposals.”
“More significantly, these response teams are the ‘farm system’ that will produce the next generation of growth leaders,” Harris adds. “A big reason for this is they have command of the process, analytics, knowledge management, and project management skills that are increasingly essential to running a modern commercial model.”
“In the average B2B organization, these bid and proposal management teams directly drive 48% of revenues – and inform the rest of the revenue equation with insights, content, and knowledge assets,” Harris continues. “They directly drive revenues by creating the proposals, bids, and documents that generate revenues. For anyone selling into long supply chains, academic, or government institutions that can represent the majority of all revenues. But what gets lost on many leaders is the contribution they can make to improving the overall go-to-market process with customer and market intelligence, advanced analytics, self-service knowledgebases, and competitive intelligence. For example, 85% of the highest performing organizations in our study (with the highest win rates and growth rates) were actively shaping the go-to-market strategies and allocation of growth resources of their organizations with revenue intelligence, signals of future demand, and fact based win-loss probabilities.”
In addition, best-in-class response teams help marketing, product and IT teams to focus and improve their efforts according to the study. For example, they help marketing teams to refine, improve, and control their positioning, messaging, and value stories – particularly in cases where RFPs make it clear a client doesn’t see their unique value and differentiation. They also help product teams better define and prioritize product roadmap requirements or promote the innovations that win deals. They help IT and operations teams to compile, curate and codify the knowledge assets, IP and “know how” in the business so it can be used in every sales and marketing interaction.
“Growth has become a team sport – and nowhere is this more evident than in the response process,” adds Harris. “Writing proposals requires input from a surprisingly large number of subject matter experts – from the CEO on down through experts from product, engineering, marketing, and IT teams. This number also includes subcontractors, legal, compliance, knowledge management, and sales enablement professionals. In addition they must also support an army of sales, account managers and distribution partners that identify, capture and follow up on client opportunities – in the form of RFPs, RFIs, Due Diligence Questionnaires as well as any client question – on a daily basis. As a consequence, bid and proposal management professionals know more about the way a company grows revenues and profits from a process and operations perspective than anyone else in a traditional functional role – in marketing, sales, or product or finance.”
Looking to the future, bid and proposal response teams are also in the best position to successfully implement and monetize corporate initiatives aimed at generating more scalable and consistent growth. This includes efforts to multiply go-to-market performance with automation, analytics and AI. For example, the Strategic Response Management (SRM) platforms they use actively consolidate the knowledge assets of a business in ways that can help every selling rep, channel and partner better respond to customers – whether it’s a simple question or a full blown RFP response. This provides a scalable foundation to build on for the 94% of commercial teams that are actively reconfiguring their commercial technology stacks in an effort to simplify the seller experience, better leverage subject matter experts, and enhance the customer experience. SRM also provides the two ingredients essential to successfully deploying and scaling AI in commercial applications. The first is a high quality proprietary learning data set to train AI. The second is a strong business case for funding AI that is tied to revenue and the customer experience. So it’s no surprise that 89% of the survey respondents were actively experimenting with ways they can use AI to automate the work of finding, assembling or creating content and improving the quality, compliance and consistency of selling proposals.
“In order to compete at the speed the modern customer expects, organizations are building commercial machines that are data-driven, technology enabled and extremely fast,” says Harris. “Add in the impact AI is having on performance, and you essentially have the commercial equivalent of a Maserati race car. The question CEOs need to be asking is who in our organization is qualified to drive that car at the speed you need to win business? The answer likely lies within your existing response team.”
“This is why a Strategic Response Management capability and skill set is so important to B2B go-to-market organizations,” says Harris. “Strategic Response Management is the people, practices, and technology that unlock organizational knowledge for profitable growth. At a fundamental level, this describes the skillset to run the modern growth engine. It is also essentially what our members have been doing for the 35 years our association has existed. They curate knowledgebases, use analytics to improve win rates, manage cross functional processes, and collaborate across dozens of stakeholders to execute revenue generating proposals. It’s like a good idea whose time has come.”
The APMP is sponsoring SRM executive summits, benchmarks, and education programs to help their members manage the growing complexity, cost and risk associated with responding to customers. This help should be welcomed because the majority of survey respondents report that responding to clients has become more labor intensive (77%), risky (64%), and competitive (52%). Almost half (46%) of bid and proposal management professionals say they are overwhelmed by collecting information and answers from many silos and systems. “You can’t manage a fast paced, data driven, and technology enabled commercial machine in 2024 using management principles from the 1960s,” says Harris.
“So it’s our job (at APMP) to shine a light on the profession and ‘uplevel’ their skills so they multiply their impact on revenue and profits and advance their careers,” says Harris. “We are looking to the future. And if you look at the evolution of business through a five to ten year lens, which we do, you will see the role of bid and proposal management professionals evolve in four important ways.
1. The emergence of dedicated response teams (or centers of excellence) to manage the increasingly large, complex and labor intensive process for responding to customer inquiries;
2. An executive in the c-suite empowered to lead the cross functional process that generates responses across the enterprise;
3. A business case for response management that puts it on equal footing with other business units in terms of ROI, contribution to firm value and financial performance;
4. A strategic basis for investment in the people, processes and technologies that will generate value and scale. These include investments in knowledgebase assets, advanced analytics, AI and technologies that improve compliance, collaboration, seller experience, and consistency.
The research paints a picture of this evolution. For example, 80% of the highest performing response teams, in terms of revenue growth and win rate, were data-driven in their approach. The vast majority (96% or more) of survey respondents identified systems and processes for aligning stakeholders, supporting greater collaboration across them, automating their efforts and helping ensure the consistency, quality and relevance of their response as critical to scaling revenues. The survey also highlighted the critical importance of building knowledgebases that capture, codify and unlock the full revenue potential of the innovations, IP and knowledge. These include the both products and solutions the business has created as well as the knowledge, ‘know how,’ intellectual property and customer insights that reside “between the ears” of their experts and customer facing employees. These “knowledge assets” represent over half of the value of the average business in an information age according to academic research.
Industry leaders also reinforce this view. “At Microsoft, our investment in an AI powered SRM platform has been crucial in managing the rapid growth of our proposal volume by providing a scalable solution that gives our expanding team streamlined access to a centralized knowledge base, allowing field teams to quickly find vetted, approved answers,” says Carrie Jordan, the Global Director of Proposals serving Microsoft’s Proposal Center of Excellence. “This has resulted in substantial productivity gains, more efficient operations, and better resource allocation because any one of the 17,000 users on our SRM platform can independently find accurate, compliant information to share with customers and prospects.”
“We view our job at the APMP is to enable the modern commercial model by helping companies win more business by adopting Strategic Response Management best practices,” says Harris. “To do this we are putting in place education, certification, partnerships, and peer networking programs focused on helping bid and proposal managers acquire and use these skills to deliver more, generate more impact, earn more, and advance their careers. If we do our job right, the business impact response teams generate will multiply, and as a byproduct you will see salaries rise, promotions happen, and collaboration across functions improve.”
As an illustration, APMP benchmarks show that bid and proposal managers that get certified in advanced skills see their salaries rise by over 25%. In addition, leaders like Dannelle Morrow and Carrie Jordan who are at the vanguard of building proposal management centers of excellence are being elevated to the C suite.
“You cannot tell the story about the business potential of Strategic Response Management without the data, which is why we worked with Responsive to create the 2024 State of Strategic Response Management Benchmark Report,” says Harris. “The data shows that companies that invest more in Strategic Response Management win more,” says Danelle Morrow, the VP of North America Creative Services and Proposal Development Center at Sodexo. “The response team holds the keys to improving the return on the overall growth investment in the business – improving response rates and sales productivity, and shrinking response times all add up to lower cost of sales and higher revenue and margin outcomes for the same invested resources. This is where APMP provides excellent resources and benchmarks to demonstrate the business case for growth – side by side comparisons of growth rate by industry, staffing levels, conversion rates, productivity, and revenue attribution benchmarks – that are critical to building the financial business case for strategic response management.”
But there is work to do. “Most leaders I speak with don’t fully understand or recognize the large contribution that response, bid and proposal management teams make to revenue growth,” says Rick Harris. “As a result, the teams that are driving half the revenues in the business are under resourced and undervalued by senior leadership.” says Rick Harris.”
A big reason response teams have been the “unsung heroes” of the revenue team is they have not been measured for their contribution to the business on the same basis as their peers in other go-to-market functions like marketing, sales, product or customer service. “A bid or proposal manager is like an “overlooked all-star” who does all the things required to win and makes all these players work better as a team,” says Harris. “They’re a lot like a point guard who doesn’t fill a stat sheet with points - but makes the passes, calls the plays, hustles on defense, and communicates. When they come on the field, the team wins. When they come off, the team gets outscored. This difference is underscored by the vast differences in win rates between world class response teams (over 60%) and low performers (under 40%).”
This “gap” between perception and reality is reflected in the big difference between senior executives and front line practitioners in terms of value to the organization and level of resources. For example, while 85% of executives feel they adequately fund their response teams, only 46% of practitioners agree. This may sound like sour grapes. But in the battle to grow revenues and share they manifest themselves in ways that materially impact revenue growth and win rates. For example, response teams at high performing firms (that win over 60% of their deals and grow year on year) have a much larger role informing go-to-market strategy, engaging C-level leaders in proposal strategy, and using data and analytics to improve revenue performance than those at lower performing organizations.
Harris believes every organization can realize significantly more performance by better organizing, measuring and managing their response teams, despite the already large impact they are having on their companies revenue growth. He also believes AI will further elevate the role of bid and response management professionals by helping them to generate more revenues, profits and the return on growth investment, knowledge assets, and human time and effort.

title: Council Post: 12 Predictions On Emerging Ways To Leverage AI In Influencer Marketing
text:
Marketers today have an abundance of AI-powered tools at their fingertips to help them ideate, build and enhance influencer marketing campaigns. Combined with a strong understanding of an organization’s goals and a solid strategy, these systems can help identify ideal collaborators, analyze content performance and even generate personalized messaging.
Below, members of Forbes Agency Council share their predictions on how AI is going to help marketing teams work more efficiently and create more impactful partnerships with social media personalities in the near future. Read on to learn about ideas for integrating AI into influencer marketing efforts to facilitate more effective and successful partnerships and campaigns.
1. AI ‘Influencers’ Will Make Real Influencers More Important
AI-generated “influencers” and “spokespeople” will be all the rage, and it will eliminate many jobs for micro-influencers. However, I predict that this will make real influencers with trust-based audiences even more important, as audiences will grow wary of AI gimmicks. Brands should foster these real connections. AI will also help to elevate the quality of content from real influencers. - Kami Watson Huyse, Zoetica
2. Influencers Using AI Will Prioritize Transparency
Influencers using AI will prioritize transparency to maintain authenticity. While AI can help influencers to produce more creative, impactful content, if the content feels fake because it’s AI-generated, they could lose credibility. Influencers build connections by relating to their audiences, and transparency around how they are leveraging AI will be crucial to maintain those audience connections. - Josh Campo, Razorfish
3. Brands Will Need To Beware Of Deepfake Technology
One thing brands need to watch out for is deepfake technology. AI does a lot of things really well. One is replicating the looks and voices of famous people. It is tempting to use this to replace having to work with an influencer at all, but people can spot a fake and will judge you harshly. Instead, focus on authenticity. Ask your influencer for their actual opinion and to use their actual likeness. - Jason Hall, FiveChannels Marketing
4. Virtual Influencers Will Allow For 24/7 Engagement
Brands can capitalize on AI-powered virtual influencers by partnering with existing virtual influencers, creating their own AI-driven brand ambassadors and using AI to optimize influencer selection and campaign performance. This will allow for 24/7 engagement, precise brand control and data-driven decision-making in influencer collaborations. - Alex Yastrebenetsky, InfoTrust
Forbes Agency Council is an invitation-only community for executives in successful public relations, media strategy, creative and advertising agencies. Do I qualify?
5. AI Will Be Used Heavily For Research And Ideation
We’re going to see AI used heavily in the research and ideation phases of influencer marketing. For research, influencer marketing hubs will utilize AI to help find the best possible matches between brand and influencer. In the ideation phase, AI will be used to help influencers come up with brand- and product-specific storyboards and scripts to shorten and dial in their production life cycle. - Yates Jarvis, 2 Visions
6. AI Will Improve Efficiency And Analysis, Not The Process
AI is not going to impact influencer marketing dramatically. This channel relies on a parasocial relationship between the influencer and the audience—something that is very human. AI can’t change or replace this relationship. So we’ll see AI being used by influencers to be more efficient and effective, and by brands to analyze performance, but the process of influencer marketing won’t change. - Mike Maynard, Napier Partnership Limited
7. Brands Will Stop Spending On Influencer Advertising
With the rise of generating your own AI avatar, brands will say goodbye to spending money on influencer advertising and instead build their own vertical using AI. Owning your own AI influencer means that there’s less risk, ultimately less cost, and you can create content quickly that you can control. - Adrian Falk, Believe Advertising & PR
8. Influencers Will Be Able To Auto-Generate UGC
AI is going to dramatically impact influencer user-generated content creation. For example, TikTok just revealed a software called Symphony that creates human-like AI-generated avatar videos. I believe influencers will eventually be able to integrate themselves into these tools to auto-generate uniquely curated content. Brands should keep an eye on this space and partner with influencers using these tools efficiently. - William Gasner, Stack Influence
9. Hyper-Niche Influencers Will Target Individual Subgroups
Get ready for a wave of AI-generated influencers. Similar to how AI-driven content is proliferating across search engines, a similar shift across social media will trigger the need for data-driven, unique, research-based content that stands out and connects specifically with its audience. This will give rise to hyper-niche influencers targeting individual subgroups. - Zamir Javer, Jumpfactor
10. Content Will Adapt To Viewers’ Preferences In Real Time
Smart brands will use AI to precisely match influencers with micro-targeted audience segments, crafting campaigns that resonate on an individual level. By implementing AI-driven, real-time performance tracking, they can develop content that adapts and shifts based on viewer preferences and behaviors. Early adoption of AI tools in influencer marketing will yield higher engagement and ROI. - Louise Mezzina, Mojo Group
11. Campaigns Will See Skyrocketing Engagement
Expect hyper-personalized campaigns with a laser focus and skyrocketing engagement. AI-generated audience insights unlock ideal micro-influencers for impactful partnerships. Embrace a data-driven approach and partner with AI platforms to gain a competitive edge. Authenticity remains key, so prioritize genuine connections. Unleash influencer marketing’s true potential with AI. - Lars Voedisch, PRecious Communications
12. AI Will Predict Audiences That Don’t Exist Yet
AI will predict audiences by using small data and predictive analysis, matching influencers and brands with developing audiences that don’t exist yet. It can also adjust content to be especially appealing to a target audience. Brands can capitalize early by investing in AI tools for precise targeting and dynamic content adjustment, ensuring they reach and engage emerging markets effectively. - Christina Mendel, EYUKO

title: AI In Hiring: 2026 Compliance Guide For Illinois Employers
text:
The increased utilization of artificial intelligence (AI) in employment practices has ushered in an era of unprecedented efficiency and innovation. However, with these advancements come new regulatory responsibilities, as demonstrated by Illinois’ recent legislative actions. On August 9, 2024, Illinois enacted HB 3773, a landmark law set to take effect on January 1, 2026, that will reshape how employers use AI in employment decisions. This legislation, amending the Illinois Human Rights Act, serves as a critical reminder that the adoption of AI in hiring, promotion, and other employment-related activities must be carefully balanced against the potential risks of discrimination and the need for transparency.
Understanding the Scope and Impact of HB 3773
HB 3773 will establish comprehensive regulations governing the use of AI in the employment lifecycle. The law broadly defines AI as any machine-based system that generates outputs such as predictions, recommendations, or decisions based on input data. This definition encompasses generative AI, which produces content that simulates human output, such as text, images, and multimedia, and more traditional predictive AI, which assists decision-making by producing scores, rankings, and classifications.
Employers in Illinois will be required to provide notice to employees, including apprentices and applicants for apprenticeship, whenever AI is utilized for key employment decisions. These decisions include recruitment, hiring, promotion, renewal of employment, selection for training or apprenticeship, discharge, discipline, tenure, or the terms, privileges, or conditions of employment. Although the law does not explicitly mention job applicants, its language suggests that AI tools used during recruitment will likely fall within its scope.
A critical component of HB 3773 is its prohibition against using AI in a manner that results in discrimination against protected classes under the Illinois Human Rights Act. Employers must also avoid using zip codes as proxies for protected classes in any AI-driven decision-making process. While the specific application of this provision remains somewhat ambiguous, it signals that employers need to be vigilant about the data inputs and algorithms used in AI systems to prevent unintentional bias.
Predictive Analysis and Geographic Discrimination
One of the more nuanced risks associated with AI in employment is the potential for predictive analysis to lead to geographic discrimination, particularly when zip codes are used as data points in AI-driven decision-making. Predictive AI systems often analyze large datasets to identify patterns and make decisions based on those patterns. However, when data points like zip codes are included, the AI may inadvertently perpetuate existing societal biases.
For example, zip codes can be highly correlated with demographic factors such as race, socioeconomic status, and education levels. In the context of recruiting, if an AI tool uses zip codes as part of its predictive analysis to rank or score candidates, it might favor candidates from certain areas over others. This could result in a form of geographic discrimination where candidates from less affluent or predominantly minority neighborhoods are unfairly disadvantaged.
Consider a scenario where an AI-driven recruitment tool is designed to predict a candidate’s likelihood of success based on various factors, including their home zip code. If the system has been trained on historical hiring data that reflects a bias toward candidates from certain zip codes—perhaps those associated with higher-income, predominantly white neighborhoods—it might rate candidates from those areas higher. Conversely, candidates from zip codes associated with lower-income or predominantly minority communities might receive lower scores, not because of their qualifications but because of the demographic characteristics associated with their geographic location.
This practice can lead to systemic exclusion of qualified candidates who happen to live in certain areas, perpetuating inequalities that the Illinois Human Rights Act seeks to address. Under HB 3773, such use of zip codes could be interpreted as a proxy for racial or socioeconomic discrimination, making it a civil rights violation.
Compliance Challenges and Best Practices
The enactment of HB 3773 reflects a broader regulatory trend that underscores the importance of responsible AI usage in employment. Employers must now navigate this evolving landscape, balancing the benefits of AI with the need to mitigate risks of discrimination and ensure transparency.
Employers should begin by conducting thorough audits of their AI systems. Regular audits can help identify potential biases that may lead to discriminatory outcomes. This process involves scrutinizing the AI-generated outputs and the underlying data inputs and algorithms. Given the broad language of HB 3773, particularly regarding the “effect of subjecting employees to discrimination,” employers should be prepared to demonstrate that their AI systems are free from bias and compliant with the new law.
Transparency is another cornerstone of HB 3773. Employers must develop clear communication strategies to inform employees and applicants about the use of AI in employment decisions. This notice should be provided at relevant stages of the employment process and should be easily understandable. Transparency not only fulfills legal requirements but also builds trust with employees and candidates, reinforcing the employer’s commitment to fair and equitable practices.
Monitoring developments from the Illinois Department of Human Rights (IDHR) will be essential as the agency issues guidance and rules related to HB 3773’s implementation and enforcement. Employers should pay close attention to any directives regarding the timing and method of notice and any additional compliance obligations that may arise.
Finally, HB 3773 does not explicitly mandate audits, but given the potential risks associated with AI-driven decisions, employers should work closely with legal counsel and experienced vendors to assess their AI systems for evidence of bias. Proactive assessments will help mitigate the risk of non-compliance and protect the organization from potential legal challenges.
The Progression of AI in Employment
As AI continues to permeate various aspects of employment, Illinois’ HB 3773 joins Colorado and New York City as another benchmark for how states may regulate this technology to prevent discrimination. Employers using AI must now navigate a complex regulatory environment that demands both innovation and caution. While the law introduces new challenges, it also provides an opportunity for employers to lead in the ethical and responsible use of AI.
Employers should view HB 3773 not just as a regulatory hurdle but as an impetus to refine their AI strategies and ensure that these powerful tools enhance fairness and inclusivity. By staying informed and taking proactive steps to comply with the law, employers can harness the benefits of AI while upholding the principles of equity foundational to a fair hiring process.
Parting Thoughts
The enactment of HB 3773 is a clear indication that Illinois is placing AI under increased scrutiny. Employers must take heed to ensure that their use of AI aligns with both legal requirements and ethical standards. The future of AI in employment is bright, but it requires a careful balance of innovation, compliance, and responsibility.

title: Author Post: Welcome to he AI Ecosystems Revolution
text:
You’ve probably heard the news: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is the next big thing, and we’re all going to be sipping mai tais on the beach while our robot overlords do the heavy lifting for us. Put a cap on that drink, friend, because we’re not quite there yet. But we are on the cusp of the AI Ecosystems Revolution.
This new concept will change the way supply chain management works and, through the power of generative AI, make us substantially more efficient.
So, what is an AI ecosystem, and how does AI fit into the logistics and supply chain ecosystem? Let’s go on a journey and figure it out together.
What Is Artificial Intelligence?
Today’s AI systems aren’t the same as those in movies with Tom Cruise and exploding trains. They are specifically termed generative AI, where a system is fed a ton of data and then, using machine learning, can provide answers to questions by predictively picking the next word in the response.
Basically, you ask it a question, and it answers.
This kind of technology can do a lot of amazing things. You’ve probably heard of ChatGPT and the cool things you can do with language, but that’s all fed by public data.
What about if you did something a little bit more specialized? What if—hear me out—you used it to solve some of the problems with the global supply chain?
What Is an AI Ecosystem?
We really need to pay attention to the ecosystem part of this equation. For this, you need not one AI-powered system but many.
This is where things get fun. How does AI fit into the logistics and supply chain ecosystem? Take a bunch of organizations and combine their data.
Think about this kind of setup:
- First, you feed your AI-powered system a whole ton of company data based on the supply chain
- Then, you have the AI analyze data, ask it questions, or use the AI system to figure out what moves to make next
- Finally, you share that data with other supply chain organizations who have followed steps one and two to create a system where people work collaboratively instead of against each other
And that, my friends, is an AI ecosystem. Multiple organizations with their AI systems are coming together to form a Voltron of information. There’s power in groups, and that’s what an AI ecosystem is all about.
How Do We Get Started With an AI Ecosystem?
This all sounds pretty easy peasy, right? But building an AI ecosystem is not something your average mom-and-pop operation can build t building an AI ecosystem is not something your average mom-and-pop operation can build in a weekend, no matter how much Red Bull you pump into their son’s veins. There are solutions, including one I’ve worked up myself.
In fact, I’ve created an assessment featuring 28 critical success factors to help you understand how prepared your company is to compete as AI ecosystems become the norm.
Are you ready to see if your company is ready to adopt AI ecosystems into its operations and customer experience? Check out a more detailed post about it here.

title: From Microsoft To Nvidia To Boston Dynamics — Here’s How AI Is Being Deployed On The Shop Floor
text:
If you own or manage a manufacturing, distribution or warehousing facility it’s time to get serious about artificial intelligence. That’s because the technology is starting to mature into something that is actually generating ROI. Software and hardware vendors are rolling out AI technologies both independently and as part of their existing products and leveraging these technologies is critical for increasing productivity, reducing overhead and increasing profits.
Here are four areas to consider.
Robotics
Manufacturing and distribution businesses of all sizes are investing heavily in AI-powered robotic technologies for the shop floor. Walmart is rolling out autonomous forklifts driven by AI software. Amazon is deploying hundreds of human-shaped warehouse robots to lift and move packages as well as independent drones to monitor traffic, safety and workflow. A German company called Robco is lending out robots that perform lathe turning laser engraving and palletizing (the robots can then be reconditioned and used for other customers as needed). Other robots are being used in food processing and baking operations to independently mix ingredients and then load finished products into cartons and cases.
Some think that humanoid robots are for the movies. But that’s not the case. They’re appearing more frequently on the shop floor – alongside and in lieu of workers.
For example, 1X creates an abundant supply of labor via safe, intelligent humanoids for the manufacturing floor. Agility Robotics is pumping out tens of thousands of humanoid warehousing robots. Boston Dynamics now makes an electric powered version of its humanoid robot Atlas. Apptronik’s Apollo is a general purpose humanoid robot designed to work in the plant and the office.
Unbox Robotics offers a bunch of AI "swarm robotics" to “accelerate the parcel sortation and order fulfillment to facilitate efficient express logistics operations delivering seamless end customer experience.” United Robots produces AI-powered robotic cleaners, disinfectors and carriers that do everything from removing microbiological contaminants to safeguarding workers to tugging heavy loads or carts. Other humanoid robots designed to perform all sorts of industrial tasks – and winning awards and - are now available (or coming soon) from companies like Figure AI and Sanctuary AI.
The robots on the manufacturing floor are controlled through the cloud using platforms provided by Nvidia (the chipmaker refers to the new platform as “a general-purpose foundation model for humanoid robots.”) and the aforementioned Agility Robotics, which the company says can “command a robot army, say, to start moving bins to a conveyor belt at a particular time.” Not sure I like the sound of that, but OK.
Internet of Things
Industry Week's VG Govindarajan and Venkat Venkatraman write that smart companies like Rolls Royce are using "fusion technology" being powered by AI is turning yesterday's equipment into thinking, intelligent machines.
"Tractors have become "farm-based computers" linked to precision agriculture cloud systems," they write. "Rolls-Royce offers "Power by the Hour" agreements for its aircraft engines. This approach ensures that Rolls-Royce is responsible for the maintenance and performance of its engines, with costs linked to the hours that the engines are in operation."
Firms with complex processing applications - particularly larger power generation, oil and gas, chemical and food and beverage manufacturing companies - are now implementing AI platforms like UptimeAI which uses sensors to monitor, analyze, evaluate and alert when there are disruptions, malfunctions or other problems that can create anomalies, loss of efficiency and safety issues.
Other software firm and hardware manufacturers are partnering to create Internet of Things (IoT) sensors that are using AI technology and models. The sensors are then installed on manufacturing equipment for the purposes of "making hardware smart" using audio, video, vision, temperature and pressure sensing.
3-D Manufacturing
A variety of companies - like Fathom Digital Manufacturing , Protolabs and Stratasys - are using AI to create 3D printing solutions to "dramatically accelerate the product development cycle" that allow manufacturers to design, create, test and evaluate prototypes in "a matter of days, rather than weeks or months."
Consolidating Data Into Large Language Models
For AI to work, large databases must be built from disparate information.
One company called EthonAI has launched a new software platform that they say "is designed to provide managers and engineers with a “sixth sense” to follow what’s happening within their factories more closely." The platform brings together data from multiple sources and then uses AI to make recommendations for management.
"With AI tools, it can be easier for companies to identify patterns that produce poor quality products and implement changes quickly," writes Rae Hartley Beck. "When a greater percentage of final products pass quality control, less waste is produced and more value is created for companies."
Another company bringing data under one roof - Sight Machine – recently announced a partnership with Siemens AG to create a manufacturing data platform for collecting, contextualizing, and analyzing all types of manufacturing data to improve production. Sight Machine’s software "analyzes the entire history of production runs to determine the best settings for the current conditions."
Microsoft announced a number of initiatives to bring data under one roof using "Copilot templates" so that their customers can "create their own copilots." The idea is for employees to use natural language queries to retrieve data - like asking the large language model why a machine is breaking and getting insights to help resolve the issues faster.
Manufacturers in the auto industry are reportedly investing in internal AI applications to help improve production scheduling, minimize line stoppage, testing chemical mixtures, aligning data from different sources to better communicate with suppliers and customers and sourcing materials based on real time availability around the world to reduce supply chain bottlenecks.
In the back office, cloud computing platform ServiceNow has released financial, customer service and operations software designed specifically for manufacturers that uses AI to do things like automatically recommend replacement parts for customer maintenance, automatically manage customer exceptions, communicate independently with suppliers and autonomously log a problem and deploy a field technician with the necessary knowledge, skills, and equipment to manage the task. Other manufacturing software makers like Epicor, SAP and Sage are rolling out similar AI based functions.
OpenAI’s ChatGPT was released in November, 2022. It created a flurry of activity, jumpstarted a tidal wave of investments, launched countless startups and forced every software and hardware company to double down on their AI offerings. Less than two years later, manufacturers are now starting to see the results of these efforts. And we’re just getting started.

title: How We Can Harness AI And AGE To Navigate Age Spurts
text:
As we navigate the complexities of life, our perception of aging evolves. At the same time science moves ahead, shedding further light on previous concepts of the underlying process. A study published this week in Nature suggests that the body doesn't age incrementally but rather in spurts, particularly during our 40s, 60s, and potentially into our 80s.
These findings offer insights not only into the physiological changes we undergo, it also puts an additional angle to look at the psychological challenges that often accompany these stages of life. For business leaders and professionals in particular it is useful to understand the intricate interplay of internal and external patterns. The more holistic our perception is, the better it can inform how we manage our careers, health, and personal aspirations over time; before we run out of it.
The Science of Aging: More Than Just a Gradual Decline
Around our mid-40s, the body begins to show signs of slowing down. We take longer to recover from illness, our wounds heal more slowly, and our metabolism decreases. For women menopause may set in. This period coincides for many with the experience of a "midlife crisis" or, more clinically, midlife depression, which is not a universal phenomenon but rather due to social factors and changes of life trajectory as shown in a 2023 study in the Lancet.
Twenty years later, in our 60s, the aging process accelerates once again, with a notable increase in the incidence of cardiovascular diseases. This period often coincides with retirement—a time when many face not only the loss of physical vitality but also the erosion of social status, and power, the weakening of professional networks, and a decrease in income and purchasing power.
The challenges of maintaining physical health become intertwined with the psychological burden of unfulfilled dreams and career pressures; whilst the experience of reduced mobility, chronic pain, and frailty darkens mental wellbeing as stressed by the World Health Organization. While the physical and the mental evolution may not be interdependent, one is influencing the other, whilst being influenced in return.
An AI-Buddy: A Companion for Healthy Aging?
In the context of these age-related challenges, where does Artificial Intelligence stand, and how could it help us? Imagine an AI companion that serves as a benevolent coach, reminding us of the passage of time—not with a wagging finger, but with gentle, encouraging nudges. This AI could keep us on track to fulfill our aspirations and long-term goals, much like a "Fitbit for Humanity."
For instance, AI could provide personalized health insights, alerting us to subtle changes in our physical condition before they become serious issues. It could remind us to engage in activities that not only maintain our physical health but also enrich our mental well-being, such as pursuing hobbies, staying socially connected, and engaging in lifelong learning. Furthermore, AI could offer prompts to reflect on our goals regularly, ensuring that we don’t lose sight of what truly matters to us amid the busyness of everyday life.
Increasingly, research shows that digital health interventions, including AI-driven apps, can improve both physical and mental health outcomes by providing timely reminders and personalized advice. For example, AI could help us manage the psychological impacts of aging by encouraging regular self-reflection on our life’s trajectory, ensuring that we continue to pursue meaningful activities that align with our core values. Protecting us from falling into the mental hamster-wheel of constant business with daily triggers to snap out of the routine that we accept all too willingly, might be a significant added value that an artificial buddy could bring.
The Pitfalls Of Neglect: Unfulfilled Potential
What makes midlife and old age depressing for some isn’t just the physical decline; it’s the realization that life has passed by without being fully lived. NIH Studies have shown that individuals who feel they have not accomplished their life goals are more prone to depression and anxiety in later years. This sense of unfulfilled potential often stems not from a lack of desire or will but from the distractions and demands of daily life—building a career, raising a family, and managing countless responsibilities.
Here’s where AI might come in. By acting as a constant, unobtrusive companion, a benevolent AI buddy could help us stay mindful of our long-term goals, even as we navigate the demands of daily life.
It’s worth noting though that while AI can be a powerful tool – but it’s not required. A simple pen and paper, combined with a few minutes of quiet reflection each day, can also help us stay on track and ensure that we’re living a life aligned with our deepest aspirations.
The AGE Strategy for Navigating Midlife and Beyond
As professionals and business leaders, it’s vital to approach aging proactively. Here are three practical takeaways, encapsulated in the acronym AGE:
- Awareness: Stay informed about the physical and psychological changes that occur as we age. Regularly assess both – your health and your life goals to ensure you’re on track, and that you are still aligned with your overall values.
- Goal Alignment: Use tools—whether AI-driven apps or traditional methods like journaling—to regularly reflect on your aspirations. Align your daily actions with these goals to ensure that you’re not just reacting to life’s demands but actively shaping your own future.
- Engagement: Maintain an active engagement with life. This means staying physically active, nurturing social connections, and continuously learning. Engage with AI and other technologies that can support your well-being, but also make time for analog activities that foster deep reflection and personal growth.
By embracing this AGE strategy, we can navigate the challenges of aging with resilience and purpose, ensuring that our later years are not marked by regret but by the fulfillment of a life well-lived, both offline and online.
