title: Council Post: Demystifying AI: Understanding The Real Impact Of Artificial Intelligence
text:
Robbie Morrison, CEO of Velosio, is a technology leader with 30+ years of experience driving business success through innovative solutions.
One of the most hyped technologies in recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), has emerged as a disruptive force for businesses, the likes of which we haven’t seen since the emergence of cloud technology. The global AI market is growing like wildfire, with projections suggesting it could reach over $1.8 trillion by 2030.
Much of what I can tell you about AI today, I wouldn’t have been able to say six months ago, and what I tell you is overhyped may be possible in six months—that's how quickly the technology is changing. There are a lot of myths and misconceptions floating around when it comes to AI, which may be holding business leaders back from adopting it.
AI Is AI—It's All The Same
Some people think that AI is the same as the other types of AI: generative AI, machine learning and deep learning. The truth is that AI is a broad field that encompasses the development of computer systems capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence. These tasks include visual perception, speech recognition, decision making and language translation.
On the other hand, generative AI, a subset of AI, refers to the ability of AI systems to generate new, original content, such as text, images, videos or audio, often in response to prompts. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) are interconnected fields representing different layers of data processing and automation. ML is a subset of AI that involves algorithms learning from data to make predictions or decisions without being explicitly programmed for the task.
DL, a further subset of ML, uses neural networks with many layers (hence "deep") to analyze data, allowing the machine to perform complex tasks like image and speech recognition. Are you confused now? Wait until the next big AI development arrives—general AI, which aims for a machine with a consciousness that can exhibit self-awareness and emotional understanding.
AI Is Going To Take Over My Job
There’s a misconception that AI will take over everyone's jobs. The truth is that AI still requires human intelligence to be effective and will enhance people’s jobs instead of replacing them. AI has the potential to automate up to 70% of employees' time spent on repetitive tasks, which can significantly boost productivity across various sectors.
At Velosio, we are looking at ways to use AI in our back office to automate tasks like collections further. That doesn't mean we will no longer need a collections manager, a controller, a staff accountant or an operations manager. We need those roles filled to interact with AI, and it allows our team to become more efficient so we can scale and grow faster.
The fear that AI could take three jobs and combine them into one is understandable. However, AI's role is to support and augment human tasks, not render them obsolete. By utilizing AI to automate repetitive tasks, employees' time is freed up to focus on higher-value, strategic tasks that will ultimately drive growth through innovation.
AI Doesn’t Require Training
Some people think anybody can use AI and get the same results, but that is not the case. For instance, generative AI combines multiple sources of information into one train of thought—but then you need to determine if it’s a valid response. After all, it’s still a computer on the other end, so you need expertise in the best ways to ask the right questions—also known as prompt engineering.
For example, when you talk with someone for the first time, you must determine how to communicate with them. Will you speak English or French? Will you speak to them like you would speak to someone with a Ph.D. or a sixth grader? It's the same with generative AI—you need to determine how to best interact with it, and a knowledgeable person can interface with it at a much higher level. This takes time, but there are also training courses on prompt engineering to get you there faster.
Quick Tip: Increase the effectiveness of your AI interactions by starting with clear and simple prompts. From there, it gradually builds complexity. This approach sets a strong baseline for your queries and will improve your skills with prompt engineering.
AI Won't Work For My Business
AI has the potential to help any business process across all industries where there are repetitive processes, undocumented processes or procedures or anything that requires hands on keyboards. Also, think about anything you currently outsource to a third party—it may make sense to let AI handle it, saving you money. For every $1 a company invests in AI, they realize an average return of $3.50 within 14 months, according to a recent study conducted by research firm IDC and sponsored by Microsoft.
Think about ways to glean more information from your data. AI could have the most impact on data analytics, and I’m excited about what some of our clients are doing in this area. AI can tap into various data sources to streamline workflows and improve sales response times. Salespeople can access the app on the go for complete customer information.
The bottom line is, don’t let myths and misconceptions hold you back from adopting AI. As it advances, the potential applications for AI in business are expanding, promising to deliver significant competitive advantages to those who adopt it. I don’t want you to miss out on efficiency gains within your company by failing to embrace the new technology.

title: Ultra-Processed Mood: Appian Injects AI Deeper Into Business Workflows
text:
Organizations run processes. At the highest level, everything in a business might be classified as a process from employee onboarding, onwards to sales outreach… and all the way down through finance and other daily operations. When the invitations go out for the staff party and the caterers get booked, there’s a process in established firms that governs the when, why and wherefore to make that thing happen.
But processes also work at a more defined level inside what is now our contemporary understanding of how a business runs. In this field, we don’t talk about peoples’ “jobs” per se, we talk about workflows, tasks, items and components. By doing so we are able to create a digitally encoded description of all the working mechanics a company operates with. With that process defined, we can then add to and subtract from it in a more controlled manner than simply getting everyone to sit at their desk and see how the day goes.
This of course is the arena of business process management, which in itself has become such a concrete de facto term that we now usually drop the “business” element (or even use the BPM acronym) and now just talk about process management.
AI, Subject To Regulations
Now more likely to describe itself as a business process specialist than refer to the cornucopia of low-code automation tools that the company is known for, Appian is now working to inject a higher degree of AI functions framed around process control into its core offering. So then, Appian Platform now expands a number of its AI capabilities, designed to enhance data and process automation for enterprises. The company says it is actively now delivering support for more enterprise AI use cases with expanded compliance, offering a framework to help organizations prepare for current and forthcoming AI regulations.
“Appian’s Copilot updates empower users to get faster answers from their enterprise data and documents, with plain language and fewer steps. AI Copilot and AI Skills also now meet HITRUST certification requirements. HITRUST certification is a security framework that provides a rigorous standardized approach to managing risk and protecting sensitive information, including compliance with HIPAA,” said Sanat Joshi, executive vice president of product and solutions at Appian.
Customers have been receptive. The Texas Department of Public Safety has used Appian to build and deploy a generative AI-powered chatbot designed to transformed the department’s procurement process.
“[Our] tool provides our procurement officials with immediate access to regulations, information and guidance on state contracting procedures, all while leveraging secure, internal data and offering precise citations. By streamlining access to critical information, the chatbot enhances efficiency and enables our staff to focus on delivering exceptional service to the public," said Michael Parks, director of procurement & contract services at the Texas Department of Public Safety.
People, Technology… and Data (or Process)
Appian has also enhanced its Appian Platform data fabric, low-code and automation capabilities. These upgrades are designed to streamline workflows by integrating “people, technology and data” into a cohesive system, allowing users to tackle business challenges more efficiently and focus on higher-impact tasks. Enterprise technology vendors love this expression and people, technology and data (and the processes that that data exists in) is used extensively as a means of expressing just how far we can now push so-called digital transformation through automation intelligence.
Appian AI enhancements in the company’s 24.3 version release include AI Copilot for data fabric, which offers insights across an enterprise data stack within a unified chat space. The company insists that AI Copilot provides “transparent and trustworthy” answers, citing its source data for verification. This tool’s cousin technology is Appian’s Enterprise Copilot, which allows users to easily extract information across curated sets of documents by asking the AI engine itself. Users are able to make these queries without what the specific document set of information is that holds the business answers they seek..
"Appian AI Copilot empowers users to explore and understand their enterprise data more effectively, using natural language and fewer steps. Now, you can ask AI Copilot questions about your entire data catalog, providing comprehensive insights and enabling more informed decision-making,” said Sanat Joshi, Executive Vice President of Product and Solutions at Appian.
Process Investigations Uncover Decisions
As part of its roadmap update at this stage, Appian has enhanced its Process HQ product (a technology designed to automate and optimize business processes) with AI-suggested starting points. This headstart is intended to speed up users’ “process investigations” by offering AI-suggested views with key performance indicators, process details and filters, ensuring the right questions are being answered… all of which investigation process should (ideally, hopefully, usually) lead to businesspeople being able to make decisions.
There’s also some love for software engineers here i.e. Appian’s AI Copilot for developers is said to help programmers test-case generation for expression rules, both making test generation faster and increasing test coverage.
Do businesses run better once they have codified themselves down into a set of processes and put digitally tracked data values on every worker, piece of machinery and every screw, carpet and door handle? Market adoption (and the general hype surrounding digital transformation) suggests that this is the way forwards. It may not completely replace gut instinct, raw human decision making and customer goodwill… but it will surely augment it from front to back.
The ultra-processed mood is generally positive in business, but ultra-processed food is still really bad for you, so go easy on the white bread and sausages please.

title: The Military Applications Of Artificial Intelligence In Space
text:
Space has long been a critical domain of military operations. But its importance is about to be amplified as artificial intelligence (AI) enables a spectrum of operations never before possible. AI, and the form of warfare it enables, Hyperwar, is more generally reshaping how nations approach military strategy and operations. The impact can be felt everywhere: from enhancing situational awareness and sensor augmentation to predictive maintenance and driving autonomous decision-making.
Let’s take a closer look at the race for dominance in the application of AI to military space applications.
First, let’s ask the obvious question. Why is space important? For one, it is the ultimate “high ground.” But the concept of space as a strategic domain also aligns with Sun Tzu's ancient principles of warfare. In "The Art of War," Sun Tzu says, "As a military force has no constant formation, water has no constant shape: the ability to gain victory by changing and adapting according to the opponent is called genius." This ancient principle finds modern application at orbital altitudes, where space assets provide both the information advantage and the response flexibility for forces acting in all domains to adapt rapidly. Satellites offer critical advantages in intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR), allowing military formations to know first, detect first, respond first, and remain ever-ready. Indeed, the very nature of space assets embodies Sun Tzu's concept of adaptability. They enable a constant state of preparedness and the ability to swiftly adjust to changing situations. With the integration of AI to fuse sensors in novel ways, extract intelligence autonomously and build predictive models of what they observe, space assets become an even greater force multiplier.
Consider the pursuit of enhanced situational awareness. In the United States, Sentient Vision Systems is pushing the boundaries of what's possible. Their ViDAR AI system, capable of detecting targets invisible to human operators or conventional radar, is a good example of how AI can bolster human capabilities in space operations.
Research at Monash University in Australia has focused on integrating deep learning models to process satellite images, significantly enhancing the speed and accuracy of detecting changes in images of objects obtained from space. These autonomous ”pattern of life” detection algorithms are becoming more and more sophisticated, providing greater insight and deeper introspection. Not only do these capabilities automate previously human analysis, thus scaling operations, they also pick up changes which were hard to detect previously, thus delivering qualitative enhancement.
China, too, is pushing forward in this area via efforts taken by the China National Space Administration (CNSA) to employ AI for analyzing satellite imagery and space debris tracking. The technology that tracks space debris can, of course, also be used to track any other type of object in orbit.
AI-driven decision-making is perhaps where the most significant changes are occurring. The U.S. Space Force is now beginning to utilize AI to accelerate decision cycles and improve strategic planning. By analyzing space-sourced datasets, AI systems can predict potential threats and optimize response strategies, delivering the adaptability Sun Tzu praised. It’s no surprise that this effort too, is being mirrored in China. Researchers at Tsinghua University have developed machine learning algorithms to process large volumes of satellite data, supporting rapid decision-making and potentially enhancing military operational efficiency.
The application of AI in predictive maintenance and maneuvering of space assets is another valuable area of investigation. The U.S. Space Operations Command (SpOC) plans to employ AI and machine learning to forecast maintenance needs, reducing downtime and enhancing efficiency. Researchers at MIT have developed models that predict satellite pattern of life. Deviations in these predictive models can indicate issues or unwelcome interventions encountered by the satellites. In China, similar advancements are being made at the Harbin Institute of Technology, focusing on AI-based predictive analytics to anticipate maintenance needs and ensure continuous operational availability of satellites.
Autonomous spacecraft and satellites are not a nice to have like an autonomous car might be. They are a must have. Distances quickly become vast once we leave the upper atmosphere. And this means significant latency for any control signals. In order to act fast, spacecraft have to act on their own. As an example of this autonomy, the U.S. Space Force is exploring AI technologies that allow satellites to y adjust their own orbits and avoid potential collisions. In China, researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences are using reinforcement learning techniques to improve satellite autonomy.
Cybersecurity in space operations is another area where AI is making significant inroads. At Cyber Command in the United States, AI systems are utilized to identify and counter cyber threats in real-time. China too is developing similar AI-driven cybersecurity systems, with research from the National University of Defense Technology emphasizing AI's ability to detect anomalies and prevent unauthorized access to sensitive space networks.
AI also has a role in facilitating better integration with allied forces. The U.S. Space Force collaborates with international partners to share AI-driven insights and intelligence. China, like the US, has recognized this potential advantage. Research being conducted at the PLA Academy of Military Science is exploring AI frameworks that enable seamless data sharing and operational coordination among Chinese and allied forces. Recent Chinese space missions such as Chang'e-6, launched on May 3, 2024, have involved the participation of multiple partner nations.
China has already established a deep space communications network and AI-driven optimization of this space-based communications backbone could be crucial for military networks. Advanced AI algorithms can manage and optimize satellite communications, handle routing and re-routing. In fact, research underway at Shanghai Jiao Tong University focuses on AI-driven communication protocols to improve the resilience and efficiency of satellite networks.
Across all these areas of application, the concept of data-driven warfare looms large. Both the United States and China are leveraging AI to manage and analyze vast amounts of data, providing timely and precise intelligence crucial for successful space missions as well as multi-domain operations enabled by space assets. There are already concrete examples of research that are aimed at cementing these advantages. Researchers at Peking University are developing AI systems that synthesize intelligence from diverse data sources, enhancing visual intelligence and reasoning as well as working on autonomy; all areas that are eminently applicable to data-centric warfare.
The integration of AI into military space operations represents a shift in how nations approach space strategy. As we've seen, this is a global phenomenon, with countries like the United States and China at the forefront, but many others joining the race. The implications of long-term autonomous systems in space, imbued with a multi-spectral view of Earth, and self-contained decision making are far-reaching. They necessarily connect with issues of national security, international cooperation, and the very nature of warfare itself. As we said earlier, space is the highest “high ground.” The decisions we make today about how we partner with other nations, and how we invest in AI in military space operations, will shape the geopolitical landscape for decades to come.
We must balance the pursuit of technological advantages with considerations of global stability. Rapid weaponization of space and any refusal on the part of major powers to keep global interests at the forefront as they push the art of the possible, can and will lead to instability. What’s certain is that the space race of the 21st century is not just about getting to claim a first for the sake of publicity and perception. This is not about putting a man on the moon mainly to say we put a man on the moon. This time, it’s about tangible strategic benefits. And it is undeniable that many of the most important benefits are in the military domain.

title: How To Grow Agency In AI Hype- Girls Who Code CEO Tarika Barrett
text:
Less than two years since ChatGPT started a technology frenzy like no other, there is growing evidence that the hype machine is slowing down. This month, we saw a a selloff of AI-invested tech companies as part of what is now a much fuzzier picture around the cost vs. value ratio for a technology prophesied to reshape humanity. The numbers aren't adding up, and while money keeps pouring into AI, very few companies are turning a profit on the tech, which remains hugely expensive to build and run. For the first time, it seems there is air leaking from the AI bubble.
While the longer term predictions for AI remain bullish, with all major tech titans continuing to hemorrhage cash on this race, this moment of recalibration is an important one. A reminder that even a technology, predicted to be the most consequential of all time, is not immune from the basic principals of economics. Like all commercial races, AI is grounded in the basic math of supply and demand, market competition, resource allocation, and assets vs value. A message that has been largely absent in an AI race that seemed emboldened with little sense of consequence for cost or human capital.
Up until now this has been a bullish race among technology leaders, who let's face it make their own rules based on speed and specter, often with little pause for the lessons of the past especially as it relates to inclusion.
Dr Tarika Barrett, CEO of Girls Who Code, and co-chair of NY Governor Kathy Hochul's emerging technology advisory board, is more aware than most of the cost of exclusion in the tech sector. She is part of a select group tasked to help further the Governor's commitment to making New York the capital of responsible development and use of AI. She shares that in her advocacy work and her role at Girls Who Code, her goal is to help marginalized communities understand the power of mind over matter. Founded by Reshma Saujani in 2012, their mission is to equip girls with the skills they need to pursue careers in an industry where they have been largely absent and help change the image of what a computer scientist looks like. At the heart of this is a sense of possibility and agency for the future, a narrative that has been threatened by the narratives surrounding AI.
I spoke to Barrett about the rapid ascendency of AI into the psyche of young women, and her work to inspire students to grow their agency within an industry in a constant state of flux, through the lens of malleability, context, and intersectionality. A practical approach, she believes can effectively help drown out fear and focus on fledging a path to inclusion.
A malleable mindset
For Barrett, a Dr in education and long term diversity advocate, she believes the most important message we need to remind ourselves is that AI and all its hype, is a human led phenomenon. It's not something that is happening to us but rather something that we can actively shape, and academia, government, and industry have a responsibility to ensure inclusive thinking. When it comes to AI, the risks of allowing the hype to take hold are higher than ever before. At the core of the threat posed by an overconfident robot is the role of human agency. The loss of such has been a first-time fear for many, but not for the team at Girls Who Code, who have long known the costs of exclusion. Barrett says while there has been a palpable sense of displacement looming across industries, for Girls Who Code, the culture of malleable mindset is at the core of everything they do. "We have had those difficult conversations, dare I whisper, 'is coding dead?'," Barrett says, "but we teach the skill of computational thinking, and foster the courage and resilience needed to deliver on it, and none of those things are changing, in fact they are more relevant than ever before."
Barrett admits that beneath the veneer of innovation and promise of AI, the race for market dominance is coming at a high cost to diverse perspectives in an industry already shaped mainly by white men. Yet this, she says, is again a stark reminder that there has never been, and will never be, a good time to break this cycle; instead, now there is an urgent necessity. "We have to turn these challenges into possibilities and ensure diverse perspectives are reflected in the technology shaping our lives. Technology is not the problem, access is. We want our students to be ready for whatever winds blow, which is not about what you do or don't know, but a willingness to learn and adapt. AI is here to stay, and we want young girls to truly believe they can play a role in its future."
Reframing fear
For Girls Who Code board members Jeannette Gamble, and Carol Juel, their own experiences of reframing how to see opportunity in change was a prime motivator for their involvement. Juel who serves as Chief Information officer at Synchrony says that she dropped out of advanced computer science class in high school when she realized she was the only girl, and her work now is shaped by the memory of how intimidating and discouraging that was, and she is on a mission to ensure girls from all backgrounds can play an active role in the future of technology. She views AI as an exciting entry point.
Gamble, a Managing Director at Morgan Stanley shares that the fear narrative surrounding AI is a result of a dichotomy leaders can reshape, and we need to help young women reframe fear to opportunity. She shares that as a woman whose own career pushed her into spaces of self-doubt, she has learned to silence the noise and listen to herself to succeed. “AI is not new,” she says, “the fear of it is. Yet when look at it holistically, there will be much broader opportunities for women in the technology field than ever before. The most exciting thing about AI is its potential to solve problems and enhance creativity, a place where we know young women excel. I want girls to understand that when interviewing for a role, you’re going to have a technical advantage if you understand the data. It opens new pathways into the industry.’’
Invoking intersectionality
Barrett shares that this opportunity to connect technology to different passions in their lives has been a natural inclination for students, who she says are "obsessed" with AI's ethical implications and bias. "These are students who grew up in a tech-heavy world. They are not interested in tech for tech's sake; they want to understand how to use it passionately and purposefully. Whether that's tech for art, education, or social good, this generation of young women do not accept things for how they have always been. They want change, which only comes with a level of access and agency that we owe them to create."
Regarding young women, AI is already proving to have an outsized impact on issues like self-confidence and body image. We have seen the real-life impacts of deep fake nudes in school environments, to a very alarming level of beauty bias built into these applications. Barrett says that while these are deeply worrying developments, the worst possible outcome is exclusion. Young women need to break from the cycle of systemic biases and become part of the solution in developing technologies that represent them and the nuances of their own perspectives.
AI, with its potential to inspire hope or instill fear, is currently in a phase of intense hype. We have a responsibility to critically examine how this constant buzz around AI shapes our perceptions, influences societal attitudes, and affects our ability to engage with technology in a balanced and informed manner. As Tarika Barrett points out, despite its fears, AI also presents an" opportunity to pioneer new paths in an industry where the stakes have never been higher. We need diverse perspectives to realize the positive potential of AI and view it as a tool for progress, not a threat."

title: Council Post: Challenges And Solutions For Generative AI In Enterprises
text:
Sarath Babu Yalavarthi is an AVP of Product Management & Development at AT&T and a Salesforce CTA.
Generative AI can be great for business, but implementation requires careful consideration of the obstacles. Here’s a deeper dive into the top five challenges as I see them today and how I believe organizations can work to overcome them.
Data Quality And Bias
Generative AI models are data-hungry, and data quality matters. So, data bias, incompleteness or inaccuracies can have a big impact on the output. This can spread misinformation, perpetuate existing biases and create harmful stereotypes.
To mitigate these risks, data curation is key. Selecting high-quality, diverse and representative datasets often requires manual review and cleaning. Using debiasing techniques like data augmentation or fairness algorithms can help counteract biases in the data. Continuous monitoring of the generative AI model’s output is necessary to catch and fix biases or inaccuracies that emerge.
Explainability And Transparency
Generative AI models are black boxes. You can’t see the reasoning behind the output, so you can’t debug errors and ensure fairness.
To get transparency and trust in generative AI we need to prioritize explainability. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques can demystify the model’s thinking by showing you its reasoning and the key factors that are influencing the output. Counterfactuals can give you insights into what would have happened if "X" occurred and help you understand the model’s logic.
Security And Privacy
Generative AI handles sensitive data like customer information or financial records. A security breach or unauthorized access to this data is a big deal.
Encrypt data at rest and in transit, limit access to data to authorized people only, and pen-test regularly to find vulnerabilities. To protect sensitive information used for training purposes, consider anonymization techniques like tokenization or differential privacy. These obscure personal data while preserving data utility. Finally, be compliant with data privacy regulations like GDPR or CCPA to handle personal info lawfully.
Human Oversight
Although AI offers automation benefits, excessive reliance on it can lead to significant problems. Depending too heavily on AI can introduce ethical issues, such as bias and misinformation in generated content. Additionally, the absence of human oversight can result in a lack of accountability, making it unclear who is responsible for errors or misuse of the technology.
To mitigate these risks, companies should have clear guidelines for generative AI usage (ethics, data privacy, human oversight, etc.). Employee training is key to responsible AI use and being able to spot potential issues. Generative AI should be developed as a tool to augment human capabilities, not replace them entirely. A human-centered approach means AI enhances decision making without compromising accountability or ethics.
For example, Salesforce's Einstein AI uses the "human in the loop" concept, allowing humans to review and act upon AI-generated content. Human touch increases quality and accuracy, thereby driving trust.
Investment And ROI
Generative AI comes with big price tags. Developing and training these complex models requires a lot of compute power. Measuring the ROI of generative AI initiatives is hard because the benefits are often intangible, such as improved customer satisfaction or better decision-making.
Enterprises should opt for cost-effective infrastructure solutions like cloud services. Implement model compression and transfer learning to reduce compute, and create a full ROI framework that includes both tangible and intangible benefits. Track key performance indicators and compare them to benchmarks to get a better sense of the financial impact of your generative AI investments.
Conclusion
Go phased. Start with pilot projects to test the tech and its challenges in a sandbox. Prioritize use cases where generative AI can deliver the most value and focus your resources there. Invest in employee training to ensure responsible AI use and a knowledgeable workforce. Stay up to date with the rapidly changing generative AI landscape to optimize and mitigate risks. If you follow these considerations, you can set yourself up to effectively and ethically get more out of generative AI.

title: How To Use AI To Make Money In 2024, From Research
text:
Since ChatGPT was launched in 2022, Gen Z and Millennial professionals who work as freelancers and small business owners, have leaped at the opportunity to leverage AI as a means of increasing their revenue.
Although it may not be used as a direct source of income in itself, young professionals within the 18-34-year-old age group consider artificial intelligence to be an all-in-one resource that drives revenue through relieving the burden off many aspects of their work, enabling them to be more productive.
For example, in an Amex Trendex survey conducted by American Express in June 2024, which surveyed over 1,000 Gen Z and Millennial professionals, nearly six in 10 respondents stated that they currently use AI in their business, compared to 34% of Gen X and Baby Boomers. (Approximately 503 businesses were run by 10 or less workers, which would have inevitably included freelance professionals or single-person contractors as well.)
The survey's findings notably concluded that Gen Zers and Millennials mostly used AI for "automating routine tasks and cash flow analytics, while Gen-X and Baby Boomers were more likely to use it for chatbots and virtual assistants, fraud protection, and workforce management."
Across the board, nearly half of businesses surveyed agreed that because of the way they used AI, they felt more prepared and had a greater chance of standing out compared to competitors, thus increasing their chances of making more money.
When asked about their most common use cases for AI in their work lives when running their businesses, these three themes emerged:
- Analyzing customer data (39%)
- Chatbots and virtual assistants (39%)
- Content creation (33%)
Let's dig into each one further.
1. Analyzing Customer Data
Customer data analysis is an essential exercise for professionals regardless of what stage of business they are in—whether one-man bands as freelancers or managing up to 500 employees. This crucial step enables you to gain business intelligence so you can see how customers interact with your company and its services/products, what their preferences and pain points are, ways you can streamline processes to make things easier for them, and areas you can deliver better quality service. Using AI, you can not only uncover this data, but also be armed with actionable insights.
For example, Insight7 is an AI-powered tool that analyzes collections of interviews—regardless of their format—and uncovers powerful insights for high-quality decisions.
HubSpot also has a Make My Persona tool that you can use to quickly and easily generate a customer persona, enabling you to map out your services and tailor them to suit the needs of specific demographics, which saves you time and money doing guesswork and enables you to target the right clientele.
2. Chatbots And Virtual Assistants
Because of the emergence of chatbots and AI-powered customer service that provide round-the-clock support and enables rapid response and satisfaction rates, traditional customer service roles are dwindling in popularity, with a 5% decline in demand reported by the BLS (this figure may have plummeted more due to the surging popularity of chatbots since BLS published this figure).
Small business owners and freelancers can tap into the opportunity to save themselves money in the long run, as instead of hiring many customer support agents, they can provide quality answers to frequently asked questions, in a fraction of the time and cost, through using a chatbot.
Additionally, instead of hiring virtual assistants who deal with admin work such as scheduling meetings, organizing calendars, responding to and sorting through emails, etc., freelancers and other small business owner can tap into the enormous possibilities of using time management and task management apps, also known as AI productivity apps. These include Clara AI, Taskade, and ProofHub.
3. Content Creation
Perhaps one of the most popular use cases for AI when it comes to making money, and especially making money from home, is content creation. Content marketing is a $72 billion-dollar industry, and the reason it is so popular is because businesses are learning that customers care more about quality information and getting answers to their questions online, than cheesy ads shown on TV or in flyers.
Content marketing includes blogging, article writing, social media posts (written content and audio/visual content), and email newsletters. Generative AI cuts the content creation process short through helping you create entire posts (which you can fact and grammar check for quality and align it with your business tone of voice), creating article outlines, giving you content inspiration, video and audio scripts, and repurposing content as well. This works in two ways to help you make money:
First, if you are a freelance content creator (like a travel blogger) or provide content marketing services as a freelance digital marketing consultant, this saves you an enormous amount of time and gives you room to be more creative.
Second, if your business is not focused on content marketing, you can still make money from this since this is one essential avenue from which you will obtain clients. In terms of AI tools, ChatGPT is one obvious option, but there are others such as Semrush, which hosts a variety of AI content planning and content generation tools suitable for social media and other forms of digital marketing.
Ultimately, while there are several use cases for artificial intelligence, these are the three that stand out the most, in which small businesses and freelancers have experienced the most benefits in terms of revenue, quality, and productivity. From lesser-known names such as Insight7 to more popular platforms and apps such as Hubspot and ChatGPT, there are plenty of ways you can cut down on your costs and make more money as a freelancer or professional starting your own business, using AI.

title: Council Post: AI’s Next Frontier: Top Trends That Will Impact Business Growth
text:
As industries and organizations have been grappling with the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, the focus has often been, “What specific tasks or processes can AI improve for us?” While that is a productive and necessary exercise, it risks missing the forest for the trees—AI is poised to not only help businesses make discrete, micro improvements, but also to change the overall business landscape in ways that will impact everyone in the workforce, top to bottom.
Preparing your organization and your team for an AI-forward future requires knowing what’s coming—both in terms of new capabilities and possible challenges. Below, members of Forbes Technology Council discuss some of the AI trends they believe will have a significant impact on business operations and growth. Read on to learn what you need to know and do now to be ready.
1. Digital Resource Areas
Organizations will add digital resource areas, much like traditional human resource areas. They will treat AI and other digital resources as competitive and important parts of the employee base. Learning to co-work with AI tools is extremely important, and AI will change the landscape of how we recruit and retain people. - Annette Klososky, Future Point of View
2. ‘Person Plus AI’ Strategy
A significant AI trend is the “Person Plus AI” strategy, which focuses on enhancing human capabilities rather than replacing them. This approach, which has proven more successful than pure automation, serves as a force multiplier for human-derived services. Companies should adopt a growth mindset, focusing on AI not just to cut costs, but to amplify human potential. This will ensure sustainable business growth. - Evan J. Schwartz, AMCS Group

3. Purpose-Focused AI Model Matching
True ROI will only be achieved with AI when companies use solutions and partners that orchestrate and match best-fit AI models to specific use cases, weighing the purpose, cost, compute needs and effectiveness. Companies should seek out technologies that offer AI agility in model selection, which will give them the ability to pivot easily to emerging or better-performing AI solutions. - Alfred Kahn, OvationCXM
4. Integration of MLOps and LLMOps Into Platform Engineering
Integrating machine learning operations (MLOps) and large language model operations (LLMOps) workflows into platform engineering practices will accelerate AI development cycles, enhance app effectiveness, increase AI software quality and improve developer productivity, all while controlling costs. Enterprises should prepare by mapping out optimized workflows and adopting software that supports rapid AI development and seamless deployment with built-in guardrails. - Haseeb Budhani, Rafay Systems
5. Embedded AI-Powered Cybersecurity
AI embedded within the hardware of enterprise devices will enable true cybersecurity by design. AI operating within the hardware’s well-defined environment means we can shift our stance from reactive to proactive, become truly autonomous in our monitoring and response, and even detect zero-day attacks. Embracing this new approach will alleviate the strain on IT teams and business owners. - Camellia Chan, Flexxon
6. Automation Of Repetitive Work
The automation of repetitive work within enterprises will reshape team sizes and shift focus from aggregating information to direct application of information. Companies must also implement master data solutions and targeted strategies to build business identity, handle entity management and maintain regulatory compliance, all of which are crucial for performance enhancement and digital transformation. - Michael Manos, Dun and Bradstreet
7. Hyper-Personalized Customer And Employee Engagement
Hyper-personalization will change how enterprises engage with their customers and employees. Using generative AI, enterprises can identify sentiment drivers and eliminate human biases to gain a clear and accurate understanding of employee sentiments. To fully realize the potential, enterprises must address data governance, build trust and carefully manage access to personal data. - Nitesh Mirchandani, Mindsprint
8. Increased Use of ML For Decision-Making
While most of the focus thus far has been on GenAI, advanced machine learning technologies are going to give business professionals growth-driving superpowers. Whether it’s about product roadmaps or where to put marketing spend, reliable modeled insights will eliminate hesitation and time-consuming data analysis to enable quick, confident business decisions. - Cody Greco, Prescient AI
9. A Focus On Accessibility
As AI is implemented to augment the workforce, it is critical to ensure that the technology and its implementation are compliant with the Americans with Disabilities Act. Not only will this give a company the ability to better engage as loyal customers (and in new ways) the 1.2 billion people with disabilities, but it will also enable increased employment of those in the disabled community, as AI drives diverse, innovative ways of performing work. - John Walsh, III, Red Summit
10. ‘User-Built’ Experiences
AI will enable users themselves to customize and personalize their own user experiences. AI agents will allow the user of an application to build their own action scenarios based on the multiple actions they take to resolve their needs. - Maksym Mashnytskyi, BMPS Technology
11. Specialized AI Agents
AI agents will automate an increasing number of repetitive tasks, especially those that involve reading and writing. Agents that are specialized in a company’s products and values will multiply organizational output. It is important to prepare by curating data that can be used to train and test these agents. Document all decisions and move from written to electronic information as far as possible. - Jeff Mahler, Ambi Robotics
12. Developing AI Apps With A Product-Oriented Mindset
A key trend in AI that will significantly impact business growth is developing AI applications with a product-oriented mindset. Companies should prioritize real-world AI applications, focusing on rapid iteration, end-user needs and leveraging platforms that automate building, testing and deployment. This approach ensures practical, production-ready AI applications that continually improve. - Milos Rusic, deepset
13. A Focus On Leveraging AI To Generate Revenue
The intersection of revenue generation with AI presents CIOs with the leadership opportunity of a lifetime. CIOs who have someone leading AI across the enterprise are in a great position. Those who don’t should prioritize creating that position. In the meantime, there’s plenty for a CIO to do to lead the company during this transformation, including forming a revenue-specific AI council. - Rohit Shrivastava, Clari
14. A Focus On Data Quality And Management
Data quality and maturity are trending. AI systems rely heavily on high-quality data for training and validation. As AI technology advances, the demand for robust, comprehensive, clean datasets will increase. To prepare, businesses should mature their data management practices, invest in data governance and ensure they have the infrastructure to collect, store and process data efficiently. - Igor Epshteyn, Coherent Solutions
15. AI Assistance For Frontline Workers
AI as an assistive technology for frontline workers will have a massive impact on labor productivity—especially in manufacturing. Operating as a copilot, AI can identify production process inefficiencies and suggest solutions in seconds. It can also augment workers’ skills with real-time guidance via digital devices. As AI evolves, its productivity benefits will help accelerate business growth. - John Davagian, L2L
16. Agentic Architecture
Agentic architecture moves us from GPT wrapper applications to fully integrated, verticalized AI apps. The advancement of open-source LLMs, such as Llama, will lower the barrier to entry and make it cost-effective for many organizations to integrate generative AI into their apps and workflows. - Karthik Sj, LogicMonitor
17. Cognitive-Capture AI
Cognitive-capture AI will have a huge impact on businesses experiencing high turnover and an aging workforce. Knowledge-transmission methods have broken down since we have moved away from the mentor-protégé system. AI will have a huge impact by capturing all of that specialized knowledge and creating a source of truth for every process, procedure and system that anyone in a business might need to know (and learn quickly). - David Francis, Virtual Method
18. AI Investments For Both Internal And External Growth
It’s essential to tailor AI investments to foster both internal and external business growth. Currently, these investments are concentrated on the potential of future efficiency and productivity improvements. The growing tendency is to transform these improvements into a service, which can propel organic growth and introduce novel products and services for both the company and its market. - Bharath Srinivas, Accenture
19. An Increase In Cybercrime
The proliferation of AI technology is democratizing cybercrime, and it will continue to do so. Anyone with a Web connection can launch a cyberattack against an organization, and this trend will not slow down. Companies must increase cybersecurity and training spending while also giving more weight to the views of CISOs and CTOs. - Ryan Lasmaili, Vaultree
20. Avoiding Overuse Of AI
Companies should understand what AI is good for and what it is not. One or two years ago, you might have been able to get away with covers of magazines and even whole articles created by generative AI. But now, the general population is becoming more adept at spotting the use (and overuse) of AI. Instead of relying too much on AI technology, the most successful companies will be the ones that can use it seamlessly. - Alec Leeseberg, Velocity Explorations

title: Council Post: How Companies Should Think About AI For Sustainability
text:
Swati Kirti is the Senior Director of Data Science at Walmart.
With the sudden rise in artificial intelligence (AI) powered solutions for sustainability, you may wonder if this is just a trend. I’m here to say no: AI can have immensely positive impacts on your sustainability initiatives.
This is especially true for companies trying to streamline their data analytics and unveil hidden opportunities for sustainability. However, proper integration is not about plugging in new technology. AI integration requires alignment with operational changes and a robust change management approach.
Identify New Opportunities
A supply chain professional with years of experience might recognize the need for process changes. These observations are valuable indicators that serve as a starting point. However, AI can add significant depth to these insights with a data-driven approach.
For instance, if you hypothesize that a particular area has significant opportunities and waste, AI can validate this by analyzing vast amounts of operational data and utilize diverse signals, confirming whether this is indeed the case and pinpointing where improvements can be made for an optimized approach. This would take considerable time and effort without the use of AI.
Every business is unique, and sustainability can mean different things depending on your type of business. It could be using more recyclable materials, increasing production efficiency to reduce waste, improving refrigeration processes and more. The key is finding a tailored AI that could pinpoint specific areas to improve your sustainability efforts.
Sizing And Mapping Opportunities
Business are complex and usually have many touchpoints in their operations where waste can occur. Further, waste could be an outcome of process gaps, people challenges or techology gaps. For example, many processes are involved in a supply chain. If your logistics supply chain has some inefficiency, this also means there could be a lot of different pieces to the puzzle.
Once you have identified your opportunities, the next step is understanding their relative size to map your priorities. This is an important step as time and resources are generally limited and hence focusing on narrow but most impactful opportunities becomes key. This is an excellent use case for AI一estimating the size of sustainability improvements一because it requires substantial computation and advanced modeling.
AI can help streamline your sustainability initiative by making recommendations involving optimized shipment routes, improved fuel efficiency or minimizing the handling of perishable goods to minimize waste. With AI, you can sort the relative importance of your goals using a quantitative method that your stakeholders understand.
Aligning Stakeholders
With a clear picture of the relative importance of your goals, it is crucial to sit down with your stakeholders and align them on how AI works for sustainability.
Integrating AI requires strong change management. This means getting everyone on board with new ways of working. Training programs should be in place to help staff learn new processes. For AI-driven sustainability efforts to be effective, operational management must actively implement the changes recommended by AI. This involves translating AI insights into practical steps within the company’s existing processes. Operational management helps ensure that AI-driven strategies lead to real, tangible improvements in sustainability practices. Ongoing support is essential to ensure smooth transitions. A culture that embraces change can help reduce resistance and improve collaboration.
Defining Sustainable AI
According to Goldman Sachs, a single ChatGPT query uses 10 times as much energy as a Google search. This has brought notable concern to the AI space. Paradoxically, AI machine learning and neural networks are being used to unlock new opportunities for sustainability.
In 2016, Google’s DeepMind AI applied machine learning to their data centers, reducing their overall energy consumption by up to 40%. Researchers at the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputer Center are experimenting with new techniques that reduce the energy required to train new AI models by 80%. While AI technology may increase your energy usage in the short term, AI tools are constantly being developed to identify and change those patterns.
Dr. Sasha Luccioni, a renowned researcher of AI energy usage, said there are a lot of opportunities for sustainability with AI. The problem, she says, is that companies view it as a one-size-fits-all approach.
A better approach is to align AI with your strategic goals for sustainability. You can set internal guidelines on using AI and use pre-trained AI models that reduce overall energy usage across your organization. As with any technology, you should measure costs against the benefits to decide if it is a good investment for your business.

title: The Business Case For Prosocial AI
text:
Do you sometimes wish the World was different – more equitable, with abundance of resources so that everyone has a fair chance to thrive? And then you tell yourself to stop dreaming because that’s not how society works, or ever will..
Artificial intelligence is often portrayed as a double-edged sword—capable of either unlocking unprecedented opportunities or precipitating unforeseen challenges. As we navigate a constantly evolving hybrid landscape, a new paradigm is emerging: Prosocial AI. This approach to AI development prioritizes the well-being of individuals, communities, society at large and the planet that all depends on, promoting positive social behaviors, collaboration, and ethical decision-making. For businesses, harnessing Prosocial AI can not only mitigate risks but also drive sustainable growth, enhance brand reputation, and foster long-term value creation.
The Concept of Prosocial AI
Prosocial AI is rooted in the idea that technology should serve the greater good. Unlike traditional AI, which often focuses on optimizing efficiency or maximizing profits, Prosocial AI is designed to align with human values and societal goals. It operates on principles of fairness, transparency, and inclusivity, ensuring that its deployment benefits all stakeholders, not just a select few.
In practical terms, Prosocial AI systems are developed with the explicit intention of fostering positive social outcomes. This could mean anything from reducing biases in hiring algorithms to supporting mental health through AI-driven counseling platforms. The overarching goal is to create AI systems that act as catalysts for positive change, helping to build more equitable, just, and harmonious societies, with careful consideration of the planet.
Practical Examples of Applied Prosocial AI
AI in Healthcare: Improving Access and Outcomes
One of the most promising applications of Prosocial AI is in healthcare, where AI-driven tools are being used to bridge gaps in access and improve patient outcomes. For instance, AI platforms like Ada Health are revolutionizing the way people access healthcare information. By providing personalized medical advice based on user-reported symptoms, Ada Health empowers individuals to make informed decisions about their health, especially in underserved areas where access to medical professionals may be limited.
Moreover, AI is being used to combat mental health challenges, which have become increasingly prevalent in the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. Platforms like Woebot use AI to deliver cognitive behavioral therapy to users, offering real-time mental health support that is accessible, affordable, and stigma-free. By providing these services, Woebot is making mental health care more inclusive and reducing the burden on traditional healthcare systems.
Ethical AI in Recruitment: Promoting Fairness and Diversity
The recruitment process is an anotherl area where Prosocial AI is making a significant impact. Traditional hiring practices are often plagued by unconscious biases that can perpetuate inequality and limit diversity within organizations. Prosocial AI offers a solution by providing tools that promote fairness and transparency in the hiring process.
For example, Pymetrics uses AI to match candidates to roles based on their cognitive and emotional attributes, rather than relying solely on resumes or traditional qualifications. By leveraging neuroscience-based assessments, Pymetrics helps companies identify candidates who are not only qualified but also likely to thrive in a particular role, regardless of their background. This approach not only enhances diversity but also improves job satisfaction and retention rates.
AI in Education: Enhancing Learning and Inclusion
Yet another arena is Education where Prosocial AI is driving positive change. AI-driven tools are being used to personalize learning experiences, making education more accessible and inclusive for students with diverse needs. For instance, platforms like Century Tech use AI to tailor educational content to individual learning styles, helping students overcome challenges and achieve their full potential.
In addition to personalized learning, Prosocial AI is also being used to address the digital divide. Organizations like Onebillion have developed AI-driven educational apps that are designed to work on low-cost devices in resource-constrained environments. By providing high-quality educational content to children in underserved communities, Onebillion is helping to bridge the gap between privileged and underprivileged students, fostering greater equity in education.
The Business Case for Prosocial AI: The PRO Framework
For businesses, embracing Prosocial AI goes beyond just corporate social responsibility—it is a strategic move that can offer substantial benefits. By focusing on PRO—Purpose, Resilience, and Optimization—companies can leverage Prosocial AI to drive growth, enhance their reputation, and ensure long-term success.
1. Purpose-Driven Growth : The foundation of any successful Prosocial AI initiative is a clear and compelling purpose. When businesses integrate AI solutions with a strong focus on social good, they align their operations with broader societal goals, creating a purpose-driven organization. This alignment not only appeals to socially conscious consumers but also resonates with employees and stakeholders who increasingly value ethical practices.
2. Resilience and Risk Mitigation : In today’s volatile business environment, resilience is key to long-term success. Prosocial AI helps companies build resilience by addressing social challenges that could otherwise pose risks to their operations. By promoting fairness and inclusivity, AI-driven tools can mitigate the risk of reputational damage caused by biased hiring practices or discriminatory algorithms.
3. Optimization for Inclusive Impact : Prosocial AI allows companies to optimize their operations in ways that are both socially responsible and economically beneficial. By designing AI systems that cater to diverse populations, businesses can tap into new markets and expand their reach, ultimately enhancing growth potential while contributing to greater social equity.
Practical Takeaways for Business Leaders
To effectively harness the power of Prosocial AI as a business leader you may want to consider the following practical steps:
1. Start with Purpose - Clearly define the social outcomes you wish to achieve and align your AI strategy with your company’s values and long-term goals.
2. Prioritize Ethics and Transparency - Ensure that your AI systems are developed and deployed with ethical considerations at the forefront, addressing potential biases and ensuring transparency.
3. Collaborate for Impact - Work with other businesses, non-profits, and government agencies to amplify the impact of your Prosocial AI initiatives.
4. Measure and Adapt - Continuously measure the impact of your Prosocial AI projects and be willing to adapt your approach as needed.
A PROactive Choice To be Made
Prosocial AI represents a powerful opportunity for businesses to contribute to the greater good while also driving their own success. By aligning AI development with human values and societal goals through the PRO framework, companies can build more resilient, inclusive, and sustainable business models. If AI turns out to be a treasure chest or Pandora’s Box depends on all of us. We can proactively make a choice which way it goes.

title: Author Post: Building Multimodal AI: Feeling Through the Dark
text:
Imagine you’re in a dark room. Squinting, you can make out a round object in front of you. What is it? Now, imagine that you can see its outline and you can smell a citrus aroma. Do you have a better guess now? Add in the touch of a wrinkly peel, and you ascertain that the object is an orange.
As humans, we combine different types of sensory input to help us navigate the world more efficiently. We are multimodal in our perception.
Artificial Intelligence models, however, only get one input. To use the example above, they might only be able to see the roundness of the orange but not feel it. While AI models use extensive sets of data, they are often restricted to one data type.
With text, AI is able to dissect individual words and form intricate mathematical representations for each word’s meaning. For images, AI models interpret pixels and generate pictures. For sounds, they comprehend frequencies and create audio. Each data type demands a distinct methodology. Yet, to date, no AI model has been able to synthesize various kinds of data to accomplish its task.
Creating a multimodal AI model represents the next frontier in artificial intelligence.
The Hurdles of Data
To create a multimodal AI, we need systems that can integrate and understand different types of data simultaneously.
Think about how we, as humans, process information. We don’t think about the disparate inputs that make up our experience of an orange. Our brain does this automatically.
Making a system with this capability is incredibly difficult. It’s not just jamming text, images, and sounds into an input and seeing what works. The AI must be able to make these disparate data work together seamlessly.
Think of a self-driving car, a use case for AI currently being tested. The car must take in a myriad of data to function. It understands the road through its cameras, detects sounds from its environment, and interprets written signs—all at once. Achieving this level of integration is what will make future AI truly transformative.
There are, however, several roadblocks to achieving multimodal AI. One great challenge is aligning different types of data that are inherently different in nature. Another is amassing the sheer computational power required to train these models.
Once we are able to surpass these, the rewards are immense. Through this pursuit of a smarter machine, we will gain deep insights into the nature of intelligence. How will our experience of the world change through this new mode of perception known as AI?
Multimodal AI is not, however, an inevitable future. It will take hard work from technology leaders. They must continue to push the boundaries of what’s possible and not settle for a “good enough” AI. For their part, Apple has adopted an integrated mindset when it comes to AI.
While not multimodal, their recent press around Apple Intelligence promises to combine generative models with personal context. This is a good first step but there’s still more to do in our journey towards multimodal AI. It’s only a matter of time before we see what AI can really do.

title: Apple Is ‘Poised To Win’ AI Wars, But The Market Already Knew That
text:
It only took a few decades for research firm MoffettNathanson to initiate coverage on the world’s most valuable company, but this week it did, saying the company’s approach to incorporating artificial intelligence into its devices has it “poised to win” the AI wars.
The funny thing is, as MoffettNathanson noted in a 72-page research note published Monday, that victory is already priced into the stock’s price of around $225 a share, up roughly one-fourth since a mid-April funk. For a company with a market capitalization north of $3.4 trillion (with very much a capital ‘T”), that’s a gigantic jump in shareholder value already.
What set off the skyrockets ? Apple’s early June World Wide Developers Conference, where the company confirmed the tech-world rumbles of the previous couple of months: Apple would weave AI capabilities into (especially) its mobile operating system and programs, while doing so in a way that protected customer privacy and data. AI would be everywhere, but in ways that made it an organic part of the daily experience of using the computer we carry everywhere.
“By the time of their June WWDC, the broad strokes of Apple’s ‘contextual awareness’ AI strategy were already well-anticipated by the tech intelligentsia, and hence by the market as well,” MoffettNathanson analysts led by Craig Moffett wrote.
That massive upgrade in everyday capabilities for iPhone users would in turn force a massive upgrade cycle to new phones because only its two newest, top-end models (the iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max) could take advantage. Eventually, Apple would almost certainly start charging for high-powered versions of its AI software, just as Open AI and many other AI companies do already.
If the company continues its usual rollout patterns for new iPhone models and operating system updates, AI-empowered versions of both will begin arriving in mid-September, though some AI functions won’t arrive until months later.
For a company that’s still largely a hardware giant, but now has an extremely high-margin services division generating close to $100 billion a year, the potential gold mine of Apple’s AI rollout has sounded pretty sweet to the market. Up shares went, and fast.
In fact, the analysts wrote, the story Apple now can tell about its AI approach, cleverly renamed “Apple Intelligence,” is so sweet, and so widely subscribed, there’s no room for further likely near-term share gains.
“The investment case for Apple rests on one simple question: can Apple ‘win’ in AI?” MoffettNathanson wrote. “Simple to ask, that is. Not so simple to answer.”
The analysts set their target price for Apple stock at $211, $14 less than Monday’s closing price on what was a modestly down day for Apple. And the analysts are “Neutral,” their equivalent of “Hold,” on the stock.
Perhaps they just don’t quite share what a modern Alan Greenspan might rumble is the market’s irrational exuberance about the stock’s further prospects for growth. And that despite what they said is their own relatively high forecasts.
“In many cases, our estimates are above consensus,” the analysts wrote. “But sell-side consensus doesn’t fully capture the level of optimism that is embedded in Apple’s current multiple. Apple’s share price already embeds an aggressive terminal growth assumption that would seem to be significantly more generous than sell-side estimates imply.”
Apple admittedly has some enormous advantages, like those 1 billion owners of Apple devices who are very much stuck into its powerful ecosystem of interconnected device software and hardware.
The company struck an important, and historically consistent, note on how its approach protects customer data and privacy through a series of maneuvers, including keeping most inquiries either on the phone itself, or anonymized onto Apple’s own private servers. For users wigged out about the potential abuses of theoretically unbound AI services provided by companies of uncertain lineage and reliability, that approach is a balm.
The markets also like the prospect of a likely eventual launch of a high-end version of a digital assistant for, say, the going rate of $20 a month. Such a super assistant within the Apple ecosystem could be another big boost to Apple’s Services unit.
But Apple’s compelling story, the one where it appears “poised to win” the AI wars, faces some serious challenges that should temper enthusiasm at least modestly, MoffettNathanson noted.
Perhaps the single most obvious question is just how big that iPhone upgrade cycle will actually be. The analysts compared it to the “supercycle” at the start of the decade that saw millions of people replace their older handsets with models capable of receiving the much faster 5G networks that rolled out in 2021 and 2022.
“There are a host of reasons why it will be challenging for an AI upgrade cycle to match that (5G) one, particularly outside of the U.S., where a combination of regulatory hurdles and geopolitical considerations are likely to restrain Apple’s AI roll-out and adoption,” MoffettNathanson wrote. “And yet Apple’s valuation today is already substantially richer than it was for the 5G cycle.”
Headaches in China, Apple’s biggest single market, may not just be that 10-percent market dip earlier in the year. Maybe Huawei and other Chinese-made phones fall back in consumer regard there, or maybe they don’t, especially if iPhones aren’t quite as AI capable in that market as they might be elsewhere.
Then there are the drumbeats of U.S. and EU regulatory pushback on several fronts, affecting the company’s App Store profits and much else.
Apple may even get hit by a regulatory clampdown affecting one of its biggest competitor/suppliers, Alphabet’s Google. The recent U.S. antitrust ruling on Google’s dominant position in search could require it to stop paying Apple more than $20 billion a year to be the default search engine on iPhones and other devices.
That may be a “don’t-throw-me-in-the-briar-patch” moment for Google, but would be a major whack to Apple’s margins.
Google also tried to steal a march on Apple’s AI rollout this past week, launching its own Gemini AI-informed tools on its Android operating system, and heavily advertising throughout the Paris Olympics telecasts and elsewhere. Whether that too provides a mortal threat to Apple Intelligence’s potential market dominance is perhaps yet another reason for tempered enthusiasm around the world’s most valuable company.

title: Dell Technologies BrandVoice: Generative AI Keys To Success: Strategy, Creativity And Patience
text:
Generative AI is testing organizations’ resolve. Staying the course is critical.
Cooking can be fun for those who relish creating something tasty and sharing it with family and friends. Some dishes come together quickly; others must marinate for hours or even days.
For instance, you may know some folks who soak ribs in apple cider or pineapple juice, the better to tenderize the meat before it touches the heat.
Like barbecue ribs, generative AI is full of promise but it also requires a good marinade to deliver the full flavor to the business. Some GenAI initiatives may take months or years to get good results.
“The future can take awhile,” industry expert Benedict Evans noted in a recent blog. After all, it took years for Google to crack the code on search ads and a decade for the iPhone to become a juggernaut. It took 20 years—two decades—for 20% of U.S. retail to migrate online.
Okay, GenAI won’t take that long to deliver value to your business, but as an IT leader you need to remember that it’s okay to play the long game. Patience is the ultimate virtue—and your business will benefit from it.
The Democratization of Innovation
Part of GenAI’s appeal is its low barrier to adoption. Recall that when OpenAI kicked off the GenAI craze with ChatGPT in November 2022, it enabled average Joe and Jane users to chat with the ease of conducting Google searches.
Today knowledge workers are using ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Claude and many other services daily to create collateral for marketing, sales, research, messaging and other business functions.
Moreover, thanks to open-source models and tools, organizations can build a usable GenAI service for under $1 million, according to Forrester CEO George Colony. How’s that for the democratization of an emerging technology?
“It’s less about the money and more about how creative your team can be in identifying the highest-return application,” Colony wrote. “Imagination and risk-taking are the dear commodities, not money.”
Even CEOs are leaning in, with 43% implementing GenAI in their organizations to drive innovation, according to Deloitte.
The future looks more promising.
Key GenAI vendors are developing small language models to run on any device, including PCs and smartphones. LLM-fueled agents may soon be able to automate entire workflows and business processes.
It remains to be seen how these capabilities and efforts will play out, but GenAI’s ability to democratize innovation levels the playing field for more folks and organizations to get into the game.
Where is the Value?
So where is the value of GenAI? Success stories can be found in organizations such as Northwestern Medicine, Duos Technologies, the City of Amarillo in Texas and Moderna.
These institutions are using GenAI to create anything from digital assistants that help share critical information to tools that help augment railroad operations and calculate dosage administration for vaccines.
These organizations serve as beacons in using strategy, creativity and imagination to navigate new technologies tools and a burgeoning ecosystem. If they can do it, why can’t your organization?
GenAI services came from out of nowhere less than two years ago. Today they’re everywhere, influencing almost every sales motion in technology.
All this is happening as organizations are still figuring out their strategies and piloting GenAI services. Fully baked go-to-market plans with cost-to-value alignment will come in time.
But it has to marinate first—like those barbecue ribs!
Such is the normal trajectory for emerging technologies; GenAI has a future in helping every organization accelerate productivity and enhance value.
Build Your AI Factory
How can your organization realize the value of GenAI?
Data. The right approach begins with high-quality data to fuel your GenAI services, which will ideally run on premises or at the edge. Bringing the AI to your data helps reduces latency and costs while protecting your corporate IP.
Infrastructure. Your data and AI models require strong foundations. AI-enabled servers and storage help you run your applications at an optimal level.
Open Ecosystem. The burgeoning AI ecosystem includes several vendors offering open-source models and tools to help plug in gaps with validated solutions and expertise.
Professional Services. Trusted partners can advise you on how to align your business and technology needs, from strategy creation to implementation, management and scaling.
Use Cases. The AI factory is only as good as its output, which you’ll achieve through identifying, prioritizing and creating use cases that help you achieve your business outcomes.
